Market data APIs for Solana/Base/BSC mem.topic: Market data APIs for Solana/Base/BSC memecoins, with focus on historical data for backtesting — endpoints, auth, pricing, rate limits, history depth, and the cheapest path to a 20k+ launch training dataset
Market data APIs for Solana/Base/BSC mem.executive_summary: The single biggest finding: you probably should not buy an API at all for the first training run. A free, MIT-licensed HuggingFace corpus (Slinky21/Pumpfun_Memecoin_Corpus, 6.7 GB) already contains 798,430 pump.fun launches, 33.58M trades, and 26.9M pre-graduation bonding-curve snapshots at ~15s granularity over a continuous 39-day window (Jun 5 – Jul 14 2026), with labeled graduation outcomes and a quantified data-quality audit. That is 40x the 20k launches asked for, at $0. A second free HF dataset (Tr4m0ryp/trenches-pumpfun-forward-2026-08, 85,442 mints, 730,850 point-in-time observations at 75s cadence) works as a clean out-of-sample forward-validation set. Its weakness is regime coverage: both are ~1-2 months, so a model trained on them is single-regime. For full history, NoLimitNodes sells the entire pump.fun archive (genesis→now, ~14M mints, ~1.8B trades, ~38k graduations) as monthly Parquet bundles for $200/mo — download one month and cancel. Among live APIs for assembling this yourself, Solana Tracker is dramatically the cheapest: its /search endpoint accepts minCreatedAt/maxCreatedAt with limit=500, so you can enumerate historical launches by date (unique among the vendors tested — Birdeye's new_listing is capped at a 3-day window and pump.fun's own /coins listing caps out around offset 1000-10000), and /chart/{token}?type=1m plus /holders/chart/{token}?type=1m give you exactly the per-minute OHLCV + holder time series you want. ~100k requests covers 20k tokens end-to-end, which fits inside the €50/mo (~$55) Advanced plan's 200,000 req/mo in a single month. Birdeye is the next best at ~$99/mo (Starter, 5M CU) using OHLCV V3 (/defi/v3/ohlcv, up to 5000 candles/call, 60/90/120 CU tiered) — ~2.7M CU for 20k tokens — but it cannot enumerate historical launches, so you must source the mint list elsewhere. Two important negatives: Dune is effectively unusable for bulk minute OHLCV export (20k tokens x 1440 min x ~6 cols ≈ 173M datapoints ≈ 173,000 credits, versus 25,000 credits on the $399/mo Plus plan), and Flipside is dead — it sold its blockchain data business to SonarX, Flipspace ran through June 17 2026, and docs.flipsidecrypto.xyz now 301s to edisyl.com. DexScreener has no OHLCV endpoint whatsoever and is a metadata/liquidity/social source only; I verified every documented endpoint live and extracted the exact rate limits from its OpenAPI spec (60 rpm for profiles/boosts/orders/ads/metas, 300 rpm for pairs/tokens/token-pairs/search). GeckoTerminal's public API is free but hard-capped at 180 days of history (verified: a before_timestamp one year back returns HTTP 401 with an explicit upgrade message) and I measured it 429ing after ~11 rapid calls, consistent with its documented 30 calls/min. On pump.fun's own infrastructure: frontend-api.pump.fun is DEAD (Cloudflare 1016 / HTTP 530) — the live host is frontend-api-v3.pump.fun — and the genuinely useful free endpoint is swap-api.pump.fun/v2/coins/{mint}/trades, which has working cursor pagination (100/page, nextCursor+hasMore) that walks backward through a token's full trade history unauthenticated; I sustained ~3.6 pages/sec. Its sibling /v1/coins/{mint}/candles is limited to the 1000 most recent candles with no backfill parameter (I tested to/before/endTs/offset — all silently ignored), so it is useless for history. Finally, PumpPortal's "free websocket" is now only partly free: subscribeNewToken and subscribeMigration are free, but subscribeTokenTrade and subscribeAccountTrade cost 0.01 SOL per 10,000 events and require a funded key.

findings.claim: The cheapest viable path to a 20k+ launch training dataset with per-token trade-level data is $0 — a free MIT-licensed HuggingFace corpus that already exceeds the requirement 40x.
findings.detail: Slinky21/Pumpfun_Memecoin_Corpus: 798,430 launches, 33,581,765 trades, 26,934,864 pre-graduation snapshots (~15s cadence), 1,392,133 post-graduation snapshots, 5,669 labeled graduated outcomes, 5,701 migrations, 1,016,374 wallet_stats rows. Window Jun 5 – Jul 14 2026 (39 continuous days). 6.7 GB across 24 Parquet files. Graduation rate 0.71% (5,689 / 798,430). Ships with quickstart.py (duckdb only) and a KNOWN_ISSUES.md with exact row counts for every defect.
findings.actionable_for_bot: huggingface-cli download Slinky21/Pumpfun_Memecoin_Corpus --repo-type dataset. Build minute OHLCV with duckdb: SELECT mint, date_trunc('minute', to_timestamp(ts)) AS m, first(price_sol ORDER BY ts) AS o, max(price_sol) AS h, min(price_sol) AS l, last(price_sol ORDER BY ts) AS c, sum(sol_amount) AS v, count(*) AS n_trades, count(DISTINCT wallet) AS n_wallets FROM 'trades/*.parquet' GROUP BY 1,2. Join tokens.parquet for initial_top10_pct_corrected and postgard_outcomes.parquet for the label.

findings.claim: That free corpus has four quantified defects that WILL silently corrupt your model if unhandled. The dataset author documents each with exact row counts.
findings.detail: (1) Mayhem-mode 2B-supply bug: concentration percentages were computed against a hardcoded 1B supply, producing initial_top10_pct up to 200%. Affects 109,561 tokens (~12.7%). FIXED — you must use the *_corrected columns (initial_top1_pct_corrected, initial_top5_pct_corrected, initial_top10_pct_corrected, dev_buy_pct_corrected, supply_bug_corrected). (2) Bonding-curve-balance leak: 1,486 tokens with impossible concentration (median top1_pct 98.8%, up to 129.3% at top10), concentrated in a Jun 23-24 clone/factory-launch burst; top1_pct correlates 0.71 with curve balance at first trade for affected rows vs -0.02 for unaffected. UNFIXABLE — flagged via top10_pct_suspect, must be EXCLUDED not imputed. (3) sol_amount inconsistent with token_amount * price_sol, off by up to ~39,000,000x: 1,136,321 rows (3.38% of 33.58M). Detect by flagging sol_amount / (token_amount * price_sol) outside [0.01, 100]; exclude from all SOL-denominated volume/PnL. The author confirms skipping this filter fully distorts a naive top-wallet ranking. (4) NULL sol_amount/price_sol: 2,360,061 rows (7.03%), flagged via sol_price_missing. Heavily front-loaded — peaks at 33.6%/45.3% null on Jun 9-10. It is a WHOLE-TOKEN phenomenon: of ~20,300 affected mints, >99.8% have every trade null-priced. Skews to early trades (median ~20 min post-launch vs ~2.4h corpus-wide).
findings.actionable_for_bot: Hardcode these as ingestion filters: WHERE top10_pct_suspect = false AND sol_price_missing = false AND sol_amount/(token_amount*price_sol) BETWEEN 0.01 AND 100. Use only *_corrected concentration columns. Because the null-price defect is whole-token and front-loaded, dropping those rows silently drops ~20,300 tokens biased toward the first 10 days — either drop those mints entirely from the training set or add a date-of-launch control.

findings.claim: Solana Tracker's /search endpoint is the only tested API that can enumerate historical token launches by creation date. Every other vendor's discovery endpoint is capped at days.
findings.detail: GET https://data.solanatracker.io/search accepts minCreatedAt and maxCreatedAt (unix ms), market (comma-separated, e.g. 'raydium,orca,pumpfun'), sortBy (default createdAt), sortOrder (asc|desc), limit default 100 / max 500 (100 when format=full), plus page/limit offset pagination AND cursor pagination. Contrast: Birdeye /defi/v2/tokens/new_listing limits time_to to 'within the last 3 days' and limit to 1-20. Solana Tracker /tokens/latest is page 1-10 only (~1,000 tokens). pump.fun's own https://frontend-api-v3.pump.fun/coins?sort=created_timestamp works at offset=0 and offset=1000 but returns [] at offset=10000 — I verified offset=1000 only reached back ~42 minutes.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Enumerate 20k launches with 40 calls: for each day-window, GET /search?market=pumpfun&minCreatedAt={t0_ms}&maxCreatedAt={t1_ms}&sortBy=createdAt&sortOrder=asc&limit=500 and walk the cursor. Header x-api-key. Do NOT design around Birdeye new_listing or the pump.fun /coins listing for historical discovery.

findings.claim: For 20k tokens with minute OHLCV + holder time series, Solana Tracker Advanced at EUR 50 (~$55) for ONE month is the cheapest paid path, by roughly 4x over Birdeye and 8x over Bitquery.
findings.detail: Request budget: discovery via /search at limit=500 = 40 requests. Per-token OHLCV via GET /chart/{token}?type=1m&time_from=<launch>&time_to=<launch+86400> = 1-2 requests x 20,000 = 20,000-40,000. Per-token holder series via GET /holders/chart/{token}?type=1m (capped at 1000 most recent points) = 20,000. Top-holder concentration via GET /tokens/{token}/holders/top = 20,000. Trade counts (not in the chart response) via GET /trades/{token} paginated ~1-3 pages = 20,000-60,000. Total ~100,000-140,000 requests, inside the Advanced plan's 200,000/month for EUR 50. Advanced has no documented per-second rate limit, so wall-clock is bounded by your own concurrency. Compare: Birdeye Starter $99 for ~2.7M CU of equivalent work; Bitquery needs Scale $239 + Solana OHLCV archive $210 = $449/mo.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Budget one month of Solana Tracker Advanced (EUR 50), run the full 20k-token backfill in that month, export to Parquet, then downgrade to Free. Confidence is medium only because the docs do not state a max-candles cap on /chart (the sibling /holders/chart is explicitly capped at 1000 points, so assume /chart is too and chunk time_from/time_to into <=1000-candle windows).

findings.claim: Birdeye OHLCV V3 is the most CU-efficient OHLCV in the market and covers Base and BSC as well as Solana, but Birdeye cannot discover historical launches so it must be paired with an external mint list.
findings.detail: GET /defi/v3/ohlcv, max 5000 records/request, tiered CU: 60 CU for <=1000 candles, 90 CU for <=2000, 120 CU for <=5000. First 24h at 1m = 1440 candles = one 90-CU call. 20,000 tokens x 90 CU = 1.8M CU. Add token_overview (20 CU x 20k = 400k) and token_security (25 CU x 20k = 500k) = 2.7M CU total, fitting the $99/mo Starter tier (5M CU) with headroom. At Starter's 15 rps, 60,000 calls takes ~67 minutes. Documented retention by interval: 1s up to 2 weeks; 15s and 30s up to 3 months; longer intervals 'extended history' (exact 1m depth is NOT documented — verify empirically before committing). The legacy GET /defi/ohlcv is 35 CU but capped at 1000 records with next_cursor/prev_cursor/has_more pagination.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Use /defi/v3/ohlcv with mode=range, type=1m, padding=false, outlier=true, currency=usd, header x-chain. For Base/BSC set x-chain: base | bsc. Before buying, spend free-tier CU probing how far back type=1m actually returns for a token launched 12 months ago — Birdeye does not document 1m retention.

findings.claim: Dune is NOT a viable bulk export path for minute OHLCV. The credit math is off by ~7x even on the $399/mo tier.
findings.detail: Datapoints = max(rows * columns, ceil(total_bytes / 100)). 20,000 tokens x 1,440 minutes x ~6 columns = 172.8M datapoints. Export costs 1 credit per 1,000 datapoints on Free/Analyst, per 5,000 on Plus, per 25,000 on Premium. So: 172,800 credits on Analyst (which includes 4,000), 34,560 on Plus (which includes 25,000), 6,912 on Premium. Plan allowances per docs.dune.com/learning/how-tos/credit-system: Free 2,500; Analyst 4,000 at $75/mo; Plus 25,000 at $399/mo; Enterprise custom. Query execution itself is 10 credits (medium engine) or 20 (large). There is a default 250,000-datapoint cap per results call, overridable with ignore_max_datapoints_per_request=true.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Use Dune only for low-cardinality LABELS and AGGREGATES — one row per token, not one row per token-minute. Good uses: deployer histories, graduation flags, sniper-wallet cohorts, bundle detection, via pumpdotfun_solana.pump_call_buy / pump_call_create and dex_solana.trades. At 20,000 rows x 20 columns = 400k datapoints = 400 credits on Analyst, that is affordable. Never SELECT minute bars through the Dune API.

findings.claim: Flipside Crypto is dead. Any plan, tutorial, or SDK reference pointing at it is stale.
findings.detail: Flipside sold its entire blockchain data business to SonarX and pivoted to Edisyl (AI agents). Flipspace was available only through June 17, 2026. Verified directly: both https://docs.flipsidecrypto.xyz/blockchain-data/solana/overview and https://flipsidecrypto.xyz/flipspace/ return HTTP 301 to https://edisyl.com/. Historically Flipside offered free Solana core data via Snowflake Marketplace (they publicly claimed 3+ trillion rows of Solana data maintained at $1M+/yr cost, given away free) with paid plans from ~$349/mo.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Remove Flipside from the provider list. If Snowflake-delivered Solana history is wanted, evaluate SonarX (the acquirer) instead. Do not write code against the FlipsideCrypto SDK.

findings.claim: GeckoTerminal's free API is hard-capped at exactly 180 days of history, enforced with a 401, and its 30 rpm limit is bursty in practice.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: GET https://api.geckoterminal.com/api/v2/networks/solana/pools/{pool}/ohlcv/minute?aggregate=1&limit=100&before_timestamp=1755000000 returns HTTP 401 with body: 'You can only access data from the past 180 days with Public API. To access data beyond 180 days, please upgrade to the Analyst plan or above.' A request without before_timestamp at limit=1000 returned exactly 1000 minute candles spanning 2026-08-22 22:37 to 2026-08-23 15:17 (16h40m of coverage per call). Rate limit: documented 30 calls/min; I fired 40 sequential unthrottled calls and got the first 429 at call ~12, with intermittent 429s thereafter. Paid depth via CoinGecko: Analyst ($129/mo) and above reach back to September 2021 with a max 6-month range per call. Critically, the ohlcv_list rows are [timestamp, open, high, low, close, volume] — there is NO trade-count field.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Use GeckoTerminal for a FREE last-180-days backfill only. Budget 3 calls per token (1x /networks/solana/tokens/{addr}/pools to resolve the pool, 2x /ohlcv/minute at limit=1000 for the first 24h) = 60,000 calls for 20k tokens = ~33 hours at 30 rpm. Pace at 2.0s/call, not 30 in a burst. You will still need a separate source for trade counts and holders.

findings.claim: pump.fun's frontend-api.pump.fun is dead; frontend-api-v3.pump.fun is live; and the genuinely useful free historical endpoint is swap-api.pump.fun/v2/coins/{mint}/trades with working cursor pagination.
findings.detail: VERIFIED 2026-08-23. https://frontend-api.pump.fun/coins → 'error code: 1016', HTTP 530. https://frontend-api-v3.pump.fun/coins?offset=0&limit=5&sort=created_timestamp&order=DESC → 200 with 45 fields. https://frontend-api-v3.pump.fun/sol-price → 200 {'solPrice':95.30,'asOfTimestamp':...,'stale':false}. https://frontend-api-v3.pump.fun/coins/currently-live → 200. DEAD on v3: /candlesticks/{mint}, /trades/all/{mint}, /replies/{mint}, /metas/current, /coins/king-of-the-hill (all 404). swap-api: GET /v2/coins/{mint}/trades?limit=100 → 200, returns {trades:[...], pagination:{nextCursor,hasMore,limit}}; limit>100 returns 400 'limit must not be greater than 100'. I paginated 12 pages / 1,200 trades in 3.3 seconds. /v1/coins/{mint}/trades returns HTTP 410 Gone directing to v2. GET /v1/coins/{mint}/candles?interval={1s|1m|5m|15m|1h}&limit<=1000&currency={USD|SOL} → 200, but limit=1001 returns 400 'limit must not be greater than 1000', interval=1d returns 400, currency=usd (lowercase) returns 400, and crucially I tested to=, before=, endTs=, and offset= — ALL are silently ignored and the response always starts at the current minute. There is no candle backfill.
findings.actionable_for_bot: For free trade-level backfill, loop: GET https://swap-api.pump.fun/v2/coins/{mint}/trades?limit=100&cursor={nextCursor} until hasMore is false. Row fields: slotIndexId, tx, timestamp (ISO8601), userAddress, type (buy|sell), program, priceUsd, priceSol, amountUsd, amountSol, baseAmount, quoteAmount, fillPriceUsd, fillPriceSol. Resample locally into 1m OHLCV + trade counts + unique-wallet counts. Throttle to ~3 rps and expect no SLA. Never use /v1/candles for history.

findings.claim: PumpPortal's websocket is no longer fully free — trade subscriptions are metered in SOL. Only launch and migration events are free.
findings.detail: wss://pumpportal.fun/api/data?api-key=<key>. subscribeNewToken: FREE. subscribeMigration: FREE. subscribeTokenTrade {method, keys:[mint,...]}: 0.01 SOL per 10,000 events. subscribeAccountTrade {method, keys:[wallet,...]}: 0.01 SOL per 10,000 events. Both paid subscriptions require a valid PumpPortal API key AND a linked wallet funded with at least 0.02 SOL. Unsubscribe methods mirror the names. Hard operational rule from the docs: 'PLEASE ONLY USE ONE WEBSOCKET CONNECTION AT A TIME' — repeatedly opening connections causes temporary bans that expire hourly. Note: a December 2024 PumpPortal tweet says 'There is no charge to use the Data API' — that is stale; the current docs are authoritative and show the per-event pricing.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Run exactly one persistent websocket. Subscribe to subscribeNewToken (free) for launch discovery, and separately subscribeMigration (free) for graduation labels. For per-token trade streams, either pay the 0.01 SOL/10k or substitute Helius webhooks / your own Geyser. Implement reconnect-with-backoff on a single socket, never a connection pool.

findings.claim: DexScreener has no OHLCV endpoint at all. Its exact per-endpoint rate limits are 60 rpm and 300 rpm, split by endpoint family.
findings.detail: From the OpenAPI spec (openapi-spec.yml served from gitbook, linked out of docs.dexscreener.com/api/reference): 60 requests/minute on /token-profiles/latest/v1, /token-profiles/recent-updates/v1, /community-takeovers/latest/v1, /ads/latest/v1, /token-boosts/latest/v1, /token-boosts/top/v1, /orders/v1/{chainId}/{tokenAddress}, /metas/trending/v1, /metas/meta/v1/{slug}. 300 requests/minute on /latest/dex/pairs/{chainId}/{pairId}, /tokens/v1/{chainId}/{tokenAddresses}, /token-pairs/v1/{chainId}/{tokenAddress}, /latest/dex/search. All 13 verified returning HTTP 200 live. Undocumented-but-alive: /latest/dex/tokens/{tokenAddress} (legacy, 200). Blocked: io.dexscreener.com/dex/chart/amm/v3/{dex}/bars/{chain}/{pair} returns 403 behind Cloudflare. No rate-limit headers are returned in responses — you must self-meter. Pair objects carry txns as a map of timeframe → {buys, sells} for m5/h1/h6/h24, volume, priceChange, liquidity{usd,base,quote}, fdv, marketCap, pairCreatedAt, labels, boosts{active}, and info{imageUrl, websites[], socials[{platform,handle}]}.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Use DexScreener as a real-time snapshot + social-metadata + paid-promotion source, never as a history source. Batch /tokens/v1/{chainId}/{addr1,addr2,...} (comma-separated, 300 rpm) for cheap bulk enrichment. Self-meter at 300 rpm since no headers exist.

findings.claim: DexScreener /orders/v1 exposes whether a token PAID for promotion, with a timestamp — an observable, cheap, and rarely-used feature.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: GET https://api.dexscreener.com/orders/v1/solana/{tokenAddress} returned {"orders":[{"chainId":"solana","tokenAddress":"...","type":"tokenProfile","status":"approved","paymentTimestamp":1786755670601}],"boosts":[{...,"amount":1...}]}. Rate limit 60 rpm. The /token-boosts/latest/v1 and /token-boosts/top/v1 feeds (also verified 200, ~23-25 KB payloads) give the current boost leaderboard chain-wide.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Add two binary/numeric features per token: has_paid_dexscreener_profile (and seconds between pairCreatedAt and paymentTimestamp), and active_boost_amount. Poll /token-boosts/latest/v1 at 60 rpm to build a time series of who is buying attention.

findings.claim: Bitquery sells real-time and history SEPARATELY, and its Solana archive only reaches back to May 2024 — with filter restrictions that break common query patterns.
findings.detail: Self-service plans (Personal $39/100k points, Pro $79/1M, Scale $239/5M) are REAL-TIME ONLY. Solana history is an add-on: $210/mo for OHLCV, $400/mo for Token Transfers. Solana(dataset: archive) and Solana(dataset: combined) cover May 2024 to now; realtime is a rolling hours-long window. For pre-May-2024 SPL transfers you must fall back to the V1 endpoint. CRITICAL FILTER RESTRICTION on archive and combined: Trade.PriceAsymmetry, Trade.Side.AmountInUSD, Trade.AmountInUSD, Trade.PriceInUSD, and Trade.Side.Account CANNOT be used inside where: — queries fail with 'no table can query DEXTradeByToken'. They work fine as output projections. Archive/combined are also limited to DEXTradeByTokens aggregates, not arbitrary trade-level filtering.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Budget $239 (Scale) + $210 (Solana OHLCV archive) = $449/mo if you go this route. Structure every historical query as Solana(dataset: combined) { DEXTradeByTokens(...) } with Block { Time(interval:{in: minutes, count: 1}) } buckets and open:Price(minimum:Block_Slot) / close:Price(maximum:Block_Slot) / high:Price(maximum:Trade_Price) / low:Price(minimum:Trade_Price) / volume:sum(of:Trade_Amount) / count. Filter pump.fun on Dex.ProgramAddress is '6EF8rrecthR5Dkzon8Nwu78hRvfCKubJ14M5uBEwF6P'. Never put a USD field in where: — filter on native amounts and convert after.

findings.claim: NoLimitNodes is the only commercial source offering the COMPLETE pump.fun history as bulk Parquet, and it includes a priority-fee/Jito-tip table nobody else ships.
findings.detail: $200/month rolling archive, daily refreshes plus monthly immutable snapshots; 30% off at 6 months, 50% at 12; custom historical pulls quoted higher. Scale as of 2026-04-29: 14M+ tokens minted, ~1.8B trades indexed, ~38,000 graduations. Bundles are 6-15 GB/month as compressed tar.zst, Parquet + CSV, decimal- and USD-normalized against SOL price oracle data, parsed against the program IDL, genesis through last UTC midnight. Seven tables: pumpfun_creates, pumpfun_trades, pumpfun_graduations, pumpfun_creator_aggregates, pumpfun_token_lifecycle, pumpfun_priority_fees (compute-unit price, priority fee, Jito tip), pumpfun_post_graduation_trades (PumpSwap + Raydium).
findings.actionable_for_bot: If you need multi-regime history (a 39-day free corpus will not generalize), buy ONE month at $200, pull the full genesis→now bundle set, and cancel. pumpfun_priority_fees is directly usable to model realistic execution cost and slippage in the backtester — most backtests of memecoin sniping are wrong precisely because they assume free, instant fills.

findings.claim: A peer-reviewable arXiv study gives you ground-truth base rates to sanity-check any backtest, and the numbers are brutal.
findings.detail: Study period Sep 1 – Oct 1, 2025, parsed directly from the Pump.fun and PumpSwap programs: 655,770 tokens created by 243,123 distinct creator addresses. Only 4,338 reached the graduation threshold = ~0.63%. Elsewhere in the paper, 2.55% of the ANALYZED subset graduated (the subset filtered to tokens with sufficient trading activity — the two figures are not contradictory, they have different denominators). Graduation threshold ~85 SOL (~$69,000 market cap in that period). MEDIAN time-to-graduation ~4.4 MINUTES. 92.22% of tokens with sufficient trading activity exhibited dump events. Strongest predictor of graduation: reaching liquidity thresholds via FEWER trades — 'fast accumulation of liquidity through a small number of trades is the strongest predictor of graduation.' Bot-dominated tokens graduate LESS in intermediate-to-late stages. Early participation by historically profitable traders gives modest uplift but with mixed effect due to fast exits. Prolific creators show weak predictive value only at advanced curve stages. No public dataset or code URL is given in the paper.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Use 0.63% as the prior graduation rate for the full population and ~0.71% as the corroborating figure from the Slinky21 corpus — these two independent sources agree, which is a strong signal. Any backtest producing a hit rate far above this is leaking. Engineer the top feature directly: sol_liquidity_added / trade_count over the first N seconds (liquidity-per-trade), not raw volume. The ~4.4 min median time-to-graduation means your decision window is SECONDS — build features from 1s/15s buckets, not 1m, for the entry model.

findings.claim: Only two of the tested OHLCV APIs return a per-candle TRADE COUNT. GeckoTerminal does not.
findings.detail: Moralis GET https://solana-gateway.moralis.io/token/{network}/pairs/{address}/ohlcv returns 'timestamp, open, close, high, low, volume, and trade count' per candle. Birdeye token_overview returns trade[frame], buy[frame], sell[frame], uniqueWallet[frame] but only as a CURRENT snapshot across fixed frames (1m/5m/30m/1h/2h/4h/6h/8h/12h/24h), not as a historical series. GeckoTerminal's ohlcv_list rows are strictly [ts,o,h,l,c,v] — no count. Solana Tracker's /chart response is {oclhv:[{open,close,low,high,volume,time}]} — no count.
findings.actionable_for_bot: If trade counts are a required feature (they should be — the arXiv paper says trade count is the denominator of the single strongest predictor), you must either (a) use Moralis OHLCV, (b) derive counts from raw trades (free via swap-api.pump.fun/v2 or the HF corpus), or (c) accept Birdeye's snapshot frames. Deriving from raw trades is both cheapest and highest-fidelity.

findings.claim: Moralis's OHLCV endpoint is a trap on the Starter tier and requires an extra resolution call per token.
findings.detail: GET /token/{network}/pairs/{address}/ohlcv costs 150 CU per call. Starter is $149/mo for 2M CU = only ~13,300 OHLCV calls/month — not enough for 20,000 tokens even at one call each. Pro at $249/mo for 100M CU = ~666,000 calls, which is ample. Additionally the path takes a PAIR address, not a token mint: 'This endpoint requires a pair address, not a token address. To find the pair addresses for a token, use the Token Pairs endpoint.' That is a second call per token. Params: fromDate, toDate (seconds or moment.js format), timeframe 1s|10s|30s|1min|5min|10min|30min|1h|4h|12h|1d|1w|1M, currency usd|native, cursor, limit 1-1000 (default 100). Auth header X-Api-Key.
findings.actionable_for_bot: If choosing Moralis, go straight to Pro ($249/mo) — Starter cannot do the job. Budget 2 calls per token (Token Pairs + OHLCV) and cache the mint→pair map permanently.

findings.claim: Helius's Enhanced Transactions API is priced 100x a normal RPC call, which rules it out for bulk historical backfill.
findings.detail: Credit costs: standard RPC 1 credit; getProgramAccounts and archival calls 10; DAS calls 10; Enhanced Transactions API 100; Mint API 100; webhook push 1; webhook create/edit/delete 100; Priority Fee API 1. Plans: Free $0/1M credits; Developer $49/10M; Business $499/100M; Professional $999/200M; Enterprise custom (1B+). Rate limits (RPC / sendTransaction / DAS / getProgramAccounts rps): Free 10/1/2/5; Developer 50/5/10/25; Business 200/50/50/50; Professional 500/100/100/75. Extra RPC on Professional is $100 per 1 RPS. LaserStream add-ons from $400/mo on Professional. Webhooks: max 100,000 addresses per webhook, 70+ transaction type filters, types enhanced/raw/discord/devnet; webhooks at >=95% failure over 7 days (24h on free) are auto-disabled.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Use Helius for LIVE operation, not backfill: raw webhooks (lower latency, no parsing) on the pump.fun program, and DAS getTokenAccounts (10 credits) for point-in-time holder sets. Do NOT loop the Enhanced Transactions API over history — 1M parsed txs = 100M credits = the entire $499 Business tier. Free tier's 1M credits = only 10,000 enhanced calls.

findings.claim: Codex.io aggregated token bars have a hard historical floor around 2025-07-21, which likely disqualifies it for a multi-year training set.
findings.detail: The docs.codex.io/recipes/charts page states aggregated token bars data has 'limited historical data, back to timestamp 1753121580' (= 2025-07-21 UTC). getBars signature: getBars(symbol: "<tokenAddress>:<networkId>", from: <unix>, to: <unix>, resolution: "1") { o h l c t volume }. Pricing: Almost Free $0/mo after a $1 verification fee, 10,000 req/mo, 5 rps, 1 key. Growth $350/mo, 1M requests (to 10M with overage at $350/million), 300 rps / 500 burst, 5 keys, 300 WebSocket connections, includes webhooks and Live Token Events. Enterprise custom. 80+ networks, 70M+ tokens, sub-1s freshness; powers TradingView, Coinbase, Uniswap.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Before paying $350/mo, verify with the free tier whether POOL-level (as opposed to aggregated-token-level) bars go deeper than 1753121580. The doc language specifically says 'aggregated token bars', which implies pool bars may be deeper — I could not confirm. Marked medium confidence.

findings.claim: Jupiter's price and token-list endpoints moved; the widely-cited v1/v2 URLs are dead.
findings.detail: VERIFIED live 2026-08-23. WORKING: GET https://lite-api.jup.ag/price/v3?ids=<mint,...> → 200, returns per-mint {createdAt, liquidity, usdPrice, blockId, decimals, priceChange24h}. GET https://lite-api.jup.ag/tokens/v2/tag?query=verified → 200, 4,407,381 bytes, fields include id, name, symbol, icon, decimals, circSupply, totalSupply, tokenProgram, mintAuthority, dev. GET https://lite-api.jup.ag/tokens/v2/search?query=BONK → 200. DEAD: https://api.jup.ag/price/v2 → HTTP 404. https://token.jup.ag/all → connection failure (host no longer resolves through the proxy).
findings.actionable_for_bot: Use lite-api.jup.ag/price/v3 for free batch USD pricing and lite-api.jup.ag/tokens/v2/tag?query=verified (cache it, 4.4 MB) as your 'is this token Jupiter-verified' feature — Birdeye also exposes jupStrictList in token_security. The createdAt and liquidity fields on price/v3 are free enrichment. Purge any code referencing token.jup.ag or price/v2.

findings.claim: Birdeye /defi/txs/token cannot backfill deep trade history — it is hard-capped at 10,000 total items per token.
findings.detail: GET /defi/txs/token: offset max 9,999, limit range 1-50 (default 50), and the binding constraint is offset + limit <= 10,000. Params: address, tx_type (swap|add|remove|all, default swap), sort_type (desc|asc), ui_amount_mode, header x-chain. Cost 10 CU. The docs call it a 'legacy trade list' and recommend migrating to Trades - Token (V3).
findings.actionable_for_bot: Never plan a full trade backfill through Birdeye. For tokens with >10,000 trades you will silently truncate. Use swap-api.pump.fun/v2/coins/{mint}/trades (free, cursor-based, unbounded) or the bulk Parquet sources instead.

findings.claim: Birdeye token_security is the single cheapest call for the rug/concentration filters a memecoin bot actually needs.
findings.detail: GET /defi/token_security, 25 CU. Solana response fields: creatorAddress, creatorBalance, creatorPercentage; ownerAddress, ownerBalance, ownerPercentage; creatorOwnerAddress, ownerOfOwnerAddress; metaplexUpdateAuthority, metaplexOwnerUpdateAuthority, metaplexUpdateAuthorityBalance, metaplexUpdateAuthorityPercent; creationTx, creationTime, creationSlot; mintTx, mintTime, mintSlot; totalSupply; top10HolderBalance, top10HolderPercent, top10UserBalance, top10UserPercent; mutableMetadata; freezeable, freezeAuthority; transferFeeEnable, transferFeeData; nonTransferable; isToken2022; isTrueToken, fakeToken; jupStrictList; preMarketHolder (array); lockInfo (object).
findings.actionable_for_bot: Note the distinction between top10HolderPercent (includes LP/program accounts) and top10UserPercent (excludes them) — top10UserPercent is the one you want for a non-LP concentration filter. Also gate on freezeAuthority != null, mutableMetadata == true, transferFeeEnable == true, and preMarketHolder length as hard rejects. creationTime/creationSlot gives you an exact launch timestamp for aligning OHLCV windows.

findings.claim: Solana Tracker's holders chart is the only clean per-minute holder time series I found in any tested API.
findings.detail: GET https://data.solanatracker.io/holders/chart/{token}, header x-api-key. Params: type (1s|1m|1h|1d, default 1d), time_from, time_to (unix seconds). Response {holders:[{holders:int, time:int}]}. Documented limit: 'Returns up to 1000 of the most recent data points.'
findings.actionable_for_bot: With type=1m and the 1000-point cap you get 16h40m of minute-resolution holder growth per call — enough to cover the critical first ~16 hours of a launch in ONE request. Chunk with time_from/time_to for longer windows. Holder-growth velocity (d(holders)/dt over the first 5 minutes) is a feature no OHLCV-only pipeline can produce.

findings.claim: Dune has usable public Solana memecoin dashboards, but two commonly-cited ones are not publicly fetchable.
findings.detail: VERIFIED HTTP 200 unauthenticated: https://dune.com/ally/solana-memecoins and https://dune.com/novemh/solana-pumpfun. VERIFIED HTTP 403: https://dune.com/adam_tehc/pumpfun and https://dune.com/hashed_official/pumpfun (may still render in a logged-in browser; the 403 is to a bare fetch). Table naming for decoded Solana programs is <namespace>_solana.<programName>_call_<instructionName>; the pump.fun namespace in community queries is pumpdotfun_solana (e.g. pumpdotfun_solana.pump_call_buy). Core curated tables referenced by working community queries: dex_solana.trades, tokens_solana.transfers, solana.transactions. A public GitHub repo of a pump.fun deployer-behavior dashboard (launches, graduation rates, PnL, self-buys, transfers, snipers, manipulators) exists at github.com/oladeeayo/Pumpfun-Token-Deployer-Records-Dashboard and names exactly those three tables.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Fork the queries behind dune.com/ally/solana-memecoins as a starting SQL skeleton for label generation. Confidence is medium on the exact decoded table names — Dune's IDL-tables doc gives only the naming SCHEME, not an enumeration, so verify pumpdotfun_solana.* resolves before relying on it.

findings.claim: PumpArchive, despite an appealing GitHub README, is completely non-functional.
findings.detail: github.com/PumpArchive/PumpArchive advertises 'the complete historical data layer for pump.fun token launches' with an API at https://api.pumparchive.com/ and planned JS/TS, Python, Go SDKs. VERIFIED: every path probed (/, /docs, /openapi.json, /v1/tokens?limit=2, /tokens?limit=2, /health) returns HTTP 404 with body {"status":"error","code":404,"message":"Application not found","request_id":"..."}. The repo has 2 commits and no license.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Exclude entirely. Do not write an adapter.

findings.claim: Birdeye's sub-minute OHLCV retention is explicitly tiered, and 1-minute retention is undocumented — a real risk for a backtest that assumes deep 1m history.
findings.detail: Documented retention on /defi/v3/ohlcv: 1s intervals retained up to 2 WEEKS; 15s and 30s retained up to 3 MONTHS; 'longer intervals: extended history available' with no number given. The Data Accessibility by Packages page enumerates WHICH endpoints each tier can call but contains no historical lookback windows for OHLCV, trades, or holders on any tier. Separately: 'The LITE/STARTER package can only access the multiple price API; all other multiple APIs are not accessible' and 'All other batch, multi/multiple APIs are available exclusively for the BUSINESS package and higher.'
findings.actionable_for_bot: Two consequences. (1) Before buying Birdeye for backtesting, empirically probe type=1m depth on a 12-month-old token using free-tier CU. (2) If your pipeline depends on Birdeye BATCH/multi endpoints to cut call counts, you need the $499 Business tier, not Starter — this can silently blow up your cost model.

findings.claim: Sources disagree materially on Dune's plan names and prices; treat any quoted Dune figure as stale.
findings.detail: docs.dune.com/learning/how-tos/credit-system: Free 2,500 credits; Analyst 4,000 credits at $75/mo; Plus 25,000 credits at $399/mo; Enterprise custom; cost per 100 credits ranging $1.396 to $5.00. Secondary/aggregator sources describe a different ladder: Free, Plus ~$390/mo, Premium ~$1,990/mo, Enterprise — with no 'Analyst' tier. Dune's own blog documents at least one credit-model change ('How you spend credits on Dune is changing'). Dune's docs also state 'we don't share a single, per-query formula because credit usage depends on real-time factors' and 'You'll see costs after execution.'
findings.actionable_for_bot: Do not hardcode Dune costs. Instrument every API response for the credit-cost field and enforce a hard monthly credit budget in code with a circuit breaker, since Dune bills post-execution and will not tell you the cost in advance.

findings.claim: CoinGecko/GeckoTerminal now expose SECOND-level onchain OHLCV aggregates, which is new and materially useful for launch-second modeling.
findings.detail: The /onchain/networks/{network}/pools/{pool_address}/ohlcv/{timeframe} endpoint accepts timeframe = day | hour | minute | second, with aggregate values of day:1; hour:1,4,12; minute:1,5,15; second:1,15,30. limit max 1000, default 100. Also supports include_empty_intervals (default false), currency usd|token, token base|quote|<address>, before_timestamp.
findings.actionable_for_bot: For entry-timing research (median graduation is ~4.4 minutes, so the decision window is seconds), request timeframe=second&aggregate=1&limit=1000 to get the first 16m40s of a launch at 1-second resolution. Set include_empty_intervals=true so your feature vectors are dense and gaps are explicit zeros rather than missing rows. Medium confidence that second-granularity is available on the FREE public host — the 180-day/Analyst gating language may also apply here; test before building.

numeric_parameters.rationale: Two independent sources one year apart agree within 13%. Use 0.007 as the prior positive-class rate. Any backtest strategy showing a hit rate materially above this without a corresponding filter that shrinks the candidate pool is leaking future information.
Hard protocol-level threshold from the arXiv study; use as the terminal condition label in the bonding-curve phase.
From the arXiv study. Your entry decision window is SECONDS, not minutes. Feature buckets must be 1s or 15s for the entry model; 1m bars are already too coarse for the median winner.
92.22% of tokens with sufficient trading activity exhibited a dump event (arXiv). Model exit/stop-loss as the default outcome, not the exception.
Bitquery documents graduation to PumpSwap as Pool.Base.PostAmount == 206900000. Use as an exact, cheap on-chain graduation detector.

Bitquery's documented formula. 793,100,000 = 1,000,000,000 - 206,900,000. NOTE: pump.fun Mayhem-mode tokens mint 2,000,000,000 supply, so this formula and any 1B-supply concentration math must be branched on supply — this exact bug corrupted 109,561 rows (12.7%) of the Slinky21 corpus.
Filter key for every pump.fun query across Bitquery, Dune decoded tables, and raw RPC log subscriptions.
ATH market cap = ATH price x supply. Getting this wrong produces >100% holder-concentration values, which is the tell that your pipeline has the bug.

numeric_parameters.rationale: Request 1440 candles (24h of 1m) in one 90-CU call rather than two 60-CU calls — 90 < 120. Always right-size count_limit to the tier boundary.
Absolute ceiling on trades retrievable per token from Birdeye. Any token above 10,000 trades is silently truncated — a survivorship trap on exactly the tokens that matter.
Enforced with HTTP 401, not a soft cap. Bounds any free GeckoTerminal-based dataset to a rolling 6-month window.

numeric_parameters.rationale: Pace at 2.0 s/call with jitter. A naive 30-in-a-row burst gets ~40% 429s.
Two calls cover a 24h post-launch window; three calls cover 48h. Use for call-count budgeting.
Hard cap on swap-api.pump.fun/v2/coins/{mint}/trades. Budget ceil(trade_count/100) requests per token.
Measured over 12 sequential pages (1,200 trades in 3.3s). Unofficial and unguaranteed — throttle to ~3 rps and implement 429/5xx backoff.
limit=1001 returns 400. to/before/endTs/offset are all silently ignored. Rules out /v1/candles for any historical dataset.

numeric_parameters.rationale: From the OpenAPI spec. No rate-limit headers are returned, so you must self-meter with two separate token buckets.
20,000 launches = 40 requests. The cheapest historical launch enumeration available.
At type=1m that is 16h40m of holder history per call — one call covers the critical first ~16 hours.
Use this to precompute export cost before executing. 20k tokens x 1440 min x 6 cols = 172.8M datapoints = 172,800 credits on Analyst (which includes only 4,000).

numeric_parameters.value: 1 credit per 1,000 datapoints (Free/Analyst), per 5,000 (Plus), per 25,000 (Premium); CSV by MB: 20 (Free) / 10 (Analyst) / 2 (Plus) credits per MB
numeric_parameters.rationale: The 25x difference between Analyst and Premium rates means the optimal Dune tier depends entirely on export volume, not query count.
A guardrail against burning a month of credits in one call. Leave it ON; if you hit it, that is a signal you should not be exporting through Dune.

numeric_parameters.value: RPC 1 / getProgramAccounts 10 / archival 10 / DAS 10 / Enhanced Transactions 100 / Mint API 100 / webhook push 1 / webhook CRUD 100 / Priority Fee 1
numeric_parameters.rationale: The 100:1 ratio between Enhanced Transactions and plain RPC is the single most important number in Helius cost modeling.
One webhook can cover an entire watchlist. Webhook CRUD costs 100 credits per call, so batch address updates rather than editing per-token.

numeric_parameters.value: >=95% failure rate over 7 days (24 hours on free plans)
numeric_parameters.rationale: Your receiver must return 2xx fast. Queue-and-ack, never process synchronously, or you will lose the stream.
Starter ($149/mo, 2M CU) = only ~13,300 OHLCV calls/month. Do not select Starter for a 20k-token backfill; Pro ($249/mo, 100M CU) is the real entry point.
Hard floor on Bitquery's v2 Solana archive and combined datasets. Pre-May-2024 requires the V1 endpoint and is transfers-only.
Documented floor for aggregated token bars. Verify pool-level bars separately before paying $350/mo.
If your entry model needs 1s bars, Birdeye gives you a 2-week rolling window only — you cannot backtest 1s entries over a year through Birdeye.

numeric_parameters.value: 14M+ mints, ~1.8B trades, ~38,000 graduations as of 2026-04-29; bundles 6-15 GB/month tar.zst
numeric_parameters.rationale: Implies a lifetime graduation rate of ~0.27% (38,000 / 14,000,000) — LOWER than both the 0.63% and 0.71% windowed figures, consistent with the Slinky21 observation that the graduation rate rose ~900x over its 39-day window as platform usage grew. Your base rate is strongly non-stationary; do not train on one window and assume it transfers.

numeric_parameters.value: Exclude top10_pct_suspect (1,486 tokens); exclude sol_price_missing (2,360,061 rows / 7.03%, ~20,300 whole mints); exclude sol_amount/(token_amount*price_sol) outside [0.01, 100] (1,136,321 rows / 3.38%); use *_corrected concentration columns (109,561 tokens / 12.7% affected)
numeric_parameters.rationale: Four mandatory filters. The author states skipping the sol_amount consistency filter alone fully distorts a naive top-wallet ranking.

numeric_parameters.value: 0.01 SOL per 10,000 events; requires linked wallet funded >= 0.02 SOL
numeric_parameters.rationale: At ~$95/SOL that is ~$0.95 per million events — cheap, but no longer free. subscribeNewToken and subscribeMigration remain free.

numeric_parameters.value: exactly 1 websocket connection; violations cause hourly-expiring bans
numeric_parameters.rationale: An architectural constraint, not a suggestion. Multiplex all subscriptions over one socket.

numeric_parameters.value: 0.5% per Local trade, 1% per Lightning trade, computed pre-slippage
numeric_parameters.rationale: If routing execution through PumpPortal, this fee must be in the backtest cost model. Pre-slippage computation means realized fee percentage will differ from nominal.

traps_and_failure_modes: FLIPSIDE IS DEAD. Sold its blockchain data business to SonarX; Flipspace ended June 17 2026; docs.flipsidecrypto.xyz 301s to edisyl.com. Every tutorial and SDK reference you find is stale. Do not budget or code for it.

frontend-api.pump.fun IS DEAD (Cloudflare error 1016, HTTP 530). Most public pump.fun bot code on GitHub still points at it. The live host is frontend-api-v3.pump.fun, and even there /candlesticks, /trades/all, /replies, /metas/current, and /coins/king-of-the-hill all 404.

PumpArchive (github.com/PumpArchive/PumpArchive, api.pumparchive.com) advertises a complete pump.fun archive with an API. Every endpoint returns 404 'Application not found'. The repo has 2 commits. It does not exist as a usable service.

DexScreener has NO OHLCV endpoint. Not undocumented — absent. The io.dexscreener.com chart-bars path that some scrapers use returns 403 behind Cloudflare. Any plan that says 'get candles from DexScreener' is wrong at the architecture level.

Dune cannot bulk-export minute bars. 20k tokens x 1440 min x 6 cols = 172.8M datapoints = ~173,000 credits, versus 25,000 on the $399/mo Plus tier. Dune also bills AFTER execution and explicitly refuses to give a per-query cost formula in advance — you can burn a month of credits on one bad query. Instrument the credit field on every response and add a hard circuit breaker.

GeckoTerminal's 180-day free limit is enforced with a 401 mid-pagination, not at request validation. A backfill loop that walks before_timestamp backwards will succeed for months and then start returning 401 bodies that a naive client may parse as empty results, silently truncating your dataset at exactly 180 days.

The Slinky21 free corpus has a whole-token NULL-price defect affecting ~20,300 mints (7.03% of trades), and it is FRONT-LOADED — peaking at 33.6%/45.3% null on Jun 9-10, the first days of the window. Naively dropping null rows removes a time-biased subpopulation and will make your model look like it learned a regime it merely lost data from.

The Mayhem-mode 2B-supply bug is the canonical memecoin data bug: concentration percentages computed against a hardcoded 1B supply produce values above 100%. It hit 12.7% of the Slinky21 corpus. If YOUR pipeline computes holder concentration or market cap, branch on actual supply — do not hardcode 1,000,000,000.

Graduation base rate is strongly NON-STATIONARY. It rose ~900x across the Slinky21 corpus's 39 days, and the lifetime NoLimitNodes ratio (~0.27%) is well below both windowed measurements (0.63%, 0.71%). A model trained on any single window will have a miscalibrated prior. Use time-ordered splits and recalibrate the intercept per period; never random-shuffle split.

Birdeye /defi/txs/token silently truncates at offset+limit <= 10,000. The tokens that exceed 10,000 trades are precisely the successful ones you most want to study — this is survivorship truncation aimed at your positive class.

Birdeye does NOT document 1-minute OHLCV retention. It documents 2 weeks for 1s and 3 months for 15s/30s, then says 'extended history' for the rest. Probe empirically on free CU before assuming you can backtest a year of 1m bars.

Birdeye batch/multi endpoints require the $499/mo Business tier ('All other batch, multi/multiple APIs are available exclusively for the BUSINESS package and higher'; LITE/STARTER get only the multiple-price API). A cost model built on Starter plus batching is off by 5x.

Moralis OHLCV takes a PAIR address, not a token mint, and costs 150 CU. Starter ($149/mo, 2M CU) affords only ~13,300 calls — fewer than one per token for 20k tokens, before the extra Token Pairs resolution call.

Helius Enhanced Transactions cost 100 credits per call versus 1 for plain RPC. Backfilling 1M parsed transactions consumes 100M credits — the entire $499/mo Business allowance. Use raw webhooks and DAS (10 credits) instead.

Bitquery sells real-time and history as SEPARATE products. Subscribing to Scale ($239/mo) and expecting historical Solana OHLCV will fail — you also need the $210/mo Solana archive add-on. And archive/combined reject USD-denominated fields (Trade.AmountInUSD, Trade.PriceInUSD, Trade.Side.AmountInUSD, Trade.PriceAsymmetry) and Trade.Side.Account inside where: clauses, failing with 'no table can query DEXTradeByToken'. Filter on native amounts and convert afterwards.
Bitquery's Solana v2 archive starts May 2024. Anything earlier requires the V1 endpoint and is transfers-only, not DEX trades.
Codex aggregated token bars bottom out at unix 1753121580 (2025-07-21). At $350/mo for Growth, verify pool-level depth on the free tier first.

PumpPortal's 'free websocket' is now only free for subscribeNewToken and subscribeMigration. Trade streams cost 0.01 SOL per 10,000 events and need a wallet funded with >=0.02 SOL. A December 2024 PumpPortal tweet saying the Data API is free is stale — the current docs override it.
PumpPortal bans clients that open multiple websocket connections (bans expire hourly). A standard connection-pool or per-token-socket design will get you banned within minutes.
Jupiter's api.jup.ag/price/v2 returns 404 and token.jup.ag/all no longer resolves. Use lite-api.jup.ag/price/v3 and lite-api.jup.ag/tokens/v2/*.
DexScreener returns NO rate-limit headers. You must self-meter two separate buckets (60 rpm and 300 rpm) — there is no server feedback to back off on except the failures themselves.

pump.fun /v1/candles accepts to, before, endTs, and offset parameters WITHOUT ERROR and ignores them, always returning the most recent N candles. A backfill loop using them will happily fetch the same 1000 candles thousands of times and produce a dataset that looks full and is entirely duplicated. Always assert that returned timestamps actually moved.
Solana Tracker prices in EUR, not USD. Budget in EUR and account for FX.

No provider tested offers per-minute HOLDER history except Solana Tracker (/holders/chart, capped at 1000 points). If your model needs holder-growth velocity — which the literature suggests it should — you have exactly one API option, or you derive it yourself from raw token-account state.

GeckoTerminal and Solana Tracker OHLCV responses contain NO trade count. Only Moralis returns a per-candle trade count, and Birdeye returns counts only as current-snapshot frames. Since trade count is the denominator of the strongest published predictor (liquidity per trade), plan to derive it from raw trades rather than from any candle API.

The median time-to-graduation is ~4.4 minutes. Building the entry model on 1-minute bars discards most of the signal for the median winner. Use 1s or 15s buckets for entry features — available free from raw trades, from Birdeye v3 (1s, 2-week retention), from Solana Tracker (type=1s), and from CoinGecko onchain (timeframe=second).

Solana low-latency execution infrastruct.topic: Solana low-latency execution infrastructure for memecoin sniping: providers, priority fees, Jito tips, compute budgets, detection paths, and MEV risk on buys
Solana low-latency execution infrastruct.executive_summary: All numbers marked "MEASURED" below are my own direct on-chain measurements taken 2026-08-23 against api.mainnet-beta.solana.com around slot 441,149,399, not repeated from marketing pages. The single most important finding: pump.fun's fee market is a *local* fee market that is 100-200x the global one. Global non-zero prioritization floor was ~2,986 microlamports/CU, while the pump.fun bonding-curve program's local floor ran p50=100,002 and p75=535,714 microlamports/CU in the same 150-slot window. Sampling 272 successful pump.fun transactions from 14 full blocks, landed cu_price was p50=264,166, p75=812,534, p90=4,000,000 and p99=40,000,000 microlamports/CU — so a competitive snipe needs roughly 1-4 million microlamports/CU, and the p50 bot is paying ~0.26 SOL-cents of priority fee, not the "medium 40,000 microlamports" that generic fee APIs return. Jito tips are a separate and thinner channel: only 12% of landed pump.fun txs carried a Jito tip at all, and among those the distribution was bimodal — p50=10,000 lamports but p90=3,000,000 and p99=5,000,000 lamports (0.003-0.005 SOL). Jito's own tip_floor API read 75th percentile = 9,523 lamports at the same moment, which is a network-wide floor and is badly misleading as a snipe target; budget 0.001-0.005 SOL for a contested mint, not 0.00001. Compute budgets: measured whole-transaction CU consumed was pump.fun bonding curve median 153,860 (min 55,587), PumpSwap AMM median 85,938, Raydium AMM v4 median 142,828, Raydium CPMM median 25,304. Set 100k CU for a warm-ATA PumpSwap buy and ~150k for a pump.fun buy including ATA creation; the sol-trade-sdk production default is exactly 150,000 CU limit / 500,000 microlamports price, which matches my measured local fee market closely. A critical and underreported finding: 77.1% of transactions touching the pump.fun bonding curve program FAIL (n=4,000), but inspecting the failures shows the dominant mode is *not* slippage — it is third-party sniper "guard" programs (e.g. 4qjYbRdexhF9hXDfzYScnzEAzE6GnUjB1RKjhEakqyu9, 7JwTi9ambvCTYwZbNQEZA8hzpG3ymPWRZpAxgKPJ94ZG) aborting with custom error 0x7 after consuming only ~950-2,750 CU. Professional snipers deliberately front their swap with a cheap on-chain precondition check so a lost race costs ~5,000 lamports base fee instead of a bad fill. You should copy this pattern. On colocation: I pulled the live leader schedule — 676 validators, 432,000 slots/epoch, strictly 4 consecutive slots per leader, top-10 leaders = 24.48% of slots, and just 40 of 676 validators produce 50% of all slots. That concentration is why multi-region submission beats single-region: you cannot colocate next to 40 validators, so you fan out. Latency ordering is settled and consistent across sources: raw shreds (sub-50ms, 100-500ms ahead of Geyser) > Geyser/LaserStream gRPC (p50 ~3ms delivery delta, ~8ms faster than `processed`) > websocket logsSubscribe > polling (2-5s). Use Geyser transactionSubscribe with a program filter as the baseline detector and shreds only if you are willing to pay $800-1,000/month/IP and handle deshredding yourself. On MEV: pump.fun's bonding curve is a constant-product curve and is fully sandwichable. Sandwich bots extracted $370-500M over Jan 2024-May 2025; the Vpe bot alone did 1.55M sandwiches in 30 days at an average of 0.0425 SOL ($8.67) profit per attack, and 16 of the top 20 sandwiched tokens were pump.fun launches. Your slippage setting is the attack surface: Jupiter's published dynamic-slippage config caps `pump_new_graduate_first_hour` at 1000-2000 bps and `degen_buy` at 1000-2500 bps, and those caps are the ceiling a sandwicher can extract. Mitigations in order of effectiveness: Jito bundles (atomic, unsandwichable within the bundle), Helius Sender with `?mev-protect=true` (routes around validators statistically linked to sandwiching), hard slippage caps, and never using a public mempool-visible path. Where sources disagree I have flagged it — notably Helius Sender's minimum tip is documented as 0.001 SOL on the current docs page but 0.0002 SOL in the zero-slot blog and in the sol-trade-sdk constant; treat 0.001 SOL as current.

findings.claim: pump.fun operates a local fee market roughly 100-200x the global prioritization fee floor; generic fee estimators will badly underprice a snipe
findings.detail: MEASURED 2026-08-23 via getRecentPrioritizationFees over a 150-slot window. GLOBAL (no account filter): only 2/150 slots non-zero, p50=2,986 microlamports/CU. pump.fun bonding curve program (6EF8rrecthR5Dkzon8Nwu78hRvfCKubJ14M5uBEwF6P): 7/150 slots non-zero, p25=2,986, p50=100,002, p75=535,714, p90/p99=714,285, max=714,285 microlamports/CU. PumpSwap AMM (pAMMBay6oceH9fJKBRHGP5D4bD4sWpmSwMn52FMfXEA): p50=27,393, p75=80,000, p90=150,000. Raydium AMM v4 (675kPX9MHTjS2zt1qfr1NYHuzeLXfQM9H24wFSUt1Mp8): p50=436,364, p75=523,034. WSOL mint as a control: 112/150 slots non-zero but p50=only 9 microlamports/CU. Helius getPriorityFeeEstimate 'medium' returns roughly 40,000 microlamports/CU which is ~13x too low for the pump.fun p75.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Never call getPriorityFeeEstimate with no accountKeys. Always pass the specific hot accounts (bonding curve PDA, pool PDA, program ID) so you get the LOCAL market. Better: run your own rolling estimator — call getRecentPrioritizationFees([<bonding_curve_pda>, <pool_pda>]) every slot, keep a 150-slot ring buffer, and set cu_price = max(p75_local, 500_000) for a contested snipe. Hardcode a floor of 500,000 microlamports/CU for any pump.fun buy.

findings.claim: Real landed pump.fun transactions pay p50=264k and p90=4M microlamports/CU; only 12% carry a Jito tip and the tip distribution is bimodal
findings.detail: MEASURED 2026-08-23: parsed 14 consecutive full blocks via getBlock, extracted every successful transaction touching the pump.fun bonding curve program (n=272), decoded ComputeBudget SetComputeUnitPrice (discriminator 0x03, u64 LE) and summed positive balance deltas to the 8 canonical Jito tip accounts. Results — cu_price microlamports/CU: p50=264,166, p75=812,534, p90=4,000,000, p99=40,000,000, max=116,999,610. Jito tips: 33/272 txs (12%) tipped at all; among tippers, lamports p50=10,000, p75=100,000, p90=3,000,000, p99=5,000,000, max=5,000,000. Total transaction fee lamports: p50=44,625, p90=1,005,000, p99=12,005,000. So the median landed pump.fun tx costs ~0.0000446 SOL all-in but the 99th-percentile competitive tx costs ~0.012 SOL.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Tier your spend by conviction. Tier 1 (routine entry, non-contested): cu_price 500,000, CU limit 150,000, no Jito tip -> ~0.000080 SOL priority + 0.000005 base. Tier 2 (contested new mint): cu_price 2,000,000 + Jito tip 1,000,000 lamports (0.001 SOL) -> ~0.0013 SOL. Tier 3 (high-conviction snipe, top-of-block): cu_price 4,000,000 + tip 3,000,000-5,000,000 lamports -> ~0.0036-0.0056 SOL. Gate Tier 3 behind an expected-value check: at 0.005 SOL/attempt you need >0.005 SOL expected profit, which at typical memecoin hit rates means position sizes of at least 0.5-1 SOL.

findings.claim: Jito's tip_floor API reports a network-wide floor that is 100-500x below what a competitive snipe actually needs — do not use it as your tip target
findings.detail: MEASURED live 2026-08-23T11:35:10Z from https://bundles.jito.wtf/api/v1/bundles/tip_floor (raw response): landed_tips_25th_percentile=1.0e-6 SOL, 50th=4.5355e-6, 75th=9.5235e-6, 95th=0.0001, 99th=0.0001 SOL, ema_landed_tips_50th_percentile=5.1567e-6 SOL. That p75 of 9,523 lamports is two to three orders of magnitude below my measured p90 pump.fun tip of 3,000,000 lamports. The API aggregates ALL bundles network-wide (including cheap arbitrage spam), not the contested-mint subset. Note the 95th and 99th percentiles both pinning at exactly 0.0001 suggests a reporting cap or rounding artifact in the endpoint. A WebSocket stream of the same data is at wss://bundles.jito.wtf/api/v1/bundles/tip_stream. Jito's documented absolute minimum tip is 1,000 lamports. Jito takes a 5% fee on tips per their own MEV report (one secondary source says 6% — Jito's own figure of 5% is more reliable).
findings.actionable_for_bot: Poll tip_floor (or subscribe to tip_stream) for a *floor sanity check only*, then apply a multiplier derived from your own observed competition. Concretely: tip = max(tip_floor_p75 * 50, 1_000_000 lamports) for a contested mint. Build your own percentile tracker instead: stream landed blocks, sum deltas to the 8 Jito tip accounts for transactions touching your target program, and maintain a rolling p75/p90 of *that* subset. This is the highest-value piece of custom telemetry you can build.

findings.claim: 77.1% of pump.fun bonding-curve transactions fail, but the dominant failure is a deliberate cheap guard-program abort, not slippage — this is a pattern to copy
findings.detail: MEASURED 2026-08-23 over n=4,000 recent signatures per program via getSignaturesForAddress. pump.fun bonding curve: 22.9% success / 77.1% fail; failure breakdown InstructionError Custom:7 = 40.4%, Custom:13 = 19.0%, Custom:3 = 11.1%, Custom:6000 = 3.6%, Custom:100 = 0.7%. Raydium LaunchLab (LanMV9sAd7wArD4vJFi2qDdfnVhFxYSUg6eADduJ3uj): 37.6% success / 62.4% fail, Custom:7 = 53.2%. PumpSwap AMM: 82.7% success / 17.3% fail (Custom:1=3.5%, Custom:5000=3.4%, Custom:1001=2.5%). Crucially, I pulled logMessages for the Custom:7/13/3 failures: they do NOT originate from the pump.fun program. They come from third-party sniper router programs — 4qjYbRdexhF9hXDfzYScnzEAzE6GnUjB1RKjhEakqyu9, 7JwTi9ambvCTYwZbNQEZA8hzpG3ymPWRZpAxgKPJ94ZG, DhpyNWkdxFh3DRPsBrwRwrK3TYC5t7Q4arnSvf3t84HY, 4F3t3Tpiyoi7Dn8oHytwJFVYJJf8cervvPL7DsZMDnCn — each consuming only 951 / 2,747 / 2,750 / 3,820 CU before failing. These are pre-condition guards that abort before the swap executes.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Deploy (or use) a thin on-chain guard program that runs FIRST in your transaction and checks: (a) bonding curve real_sol_reserves is still below your entry threshold, (b) the token was created within N slots, (c) top-holder concentration proxy, (d) your expected out-amount is still achievable. Abort with a custom error if any check fails. Cost of a lost race drops to 5,000 lamports base fee + ~3,000 CU of priority fee instead of a filled bad entry. Because the priority fee is charged on the *requested* CU limit, not consumed, keep the CU limit low on guard-heavy paths. Also note: the raw 77% failure rate means any 'landing rate' you compute must be measured against your own signatures, not the program aggregate.

PumpSwap AMM (n=11): min=7,375 median=85,938 max=163,801. Raydium AMM v4 (n=8): min=47,437 median=142,828 max=149,303. Raydium CPMM (n=14): min=20,740 median=25,304 max=109,718. Production reference: sol-trade-sdk (github.com/0xfnzero/sol-trade-sdk) constants/trade.rs sets DEFAULT_TIP_UNIT_LIMIT=150000, DEFAULT_TIP_UNIT_PRICE=500000, DEFAULT_RPC_UNIT_LIMIT=150000, DEFAULT_RPC_UNIT_PRICE=500000, DEFAULT_BUY_TIP_FEE=0.0006 SOL, DEFAULT_SELL_TIP_FEE=0.0001 SOL; its tests assert buy cu_limit=100,000 and sell cu_limit=90,000. findings.actionable_for_bot: Hardcode these CU limits: pump.fun buy with ATA creation = 160,000; pump.fun buy with warm ATA = 100,000; pump.fun sell = 90,000; PumpSwap buy = 100,000; Raydium AMM v4 swap = 150,000; Raydium CPMM = 40,000. Do NOT simulate before a snipe — simulateTransaction costs a full RTT you cannot afford. Instead precompute per-venue constants offline and add a 15% margin. Because priority fee = cu_price * cu_limit, dropping from a lazy 1,400,000 CU limit to 150,000 at 500,000 microlamports/CU saves 0.000625 SOL per attempt — at 1,000 attempts/day that is 0.625 SOL/day.

findings.claim: Live leader schedule is 676 validators, exactly 4 consecutive slots each, with 40 validators producing 50% of slots — this dictates a multi-region fan-out, not a single colocation
findings.detail: MEASURED 2026-08-23 via getLeaderSchedule. 676 validators hold slots; 432,000 slots per epoch; top-10 leaders = 24.48% of all slots; 40 of 676 validators produce 50% of slots. Sampled validator slot offsets confirm strict 4-slot runs: [24856,24857,24858,24859, 34256,34257,34258,34259, 36704,...]. At 400ms/slot a leader holds the pen for ~1.6 seconds. Slots-per-validator mode was 84-148. Geographic concentration per secondary sources: highest-stake density in Ashburn VA and NY metro, secondary clusters Frankfurt and Amsterdam (one source claims Amsterdam alone is ~a quarter of slots — I could not verify this independently, treat as low confidence), growing Tokyo/Seoul. Colocation in FRA/LON/NY reportedly achieves sub-30ms RTT to the nearest leader. A 100-150ms trans-Atlantic RTT consumes 25-35% of a 400ms slot before the RPC even forwards.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Do not pick one region. Fetch getLeaderSchedule once per epoch, map each leader identity to a region (via validators.app or your own gossip crawl of contact_info IPs -> GeoIP), and precompute a slot->region table. Submit each transaction to 2-4 regional endpoints simultaneously, always including the region matching the CURRENT and NEXT leader (you know it 4 slots ahead). Cache the schedule; it only changes each epoch (~2 days). Minimum viable footprint: one box in Frankfurt or Amsterdam plus one in NY/Ashburn. Note the 4-slot run means if you miss the current leader you have ~1.6s before the next — plenty of time to retry with a different region, so build retry-with-region-switch rather than blind resubmission.

findings.claim: Detection latency ordering: shreds < Geyser/LaserStream gRPC < websocket logsSubscribe < polling, with shreds 100-500ms ahead of Geyser
findings.detail: Decoded shreds achieve sub-50ms latency and give 'earliest bytes'. Jito ShredStream / shred-based feeds deliver transaction intent typically 100-500ms earlier than standard Yellowstone gRPC because shreds are emitted by the leader before the block is complete and before Turbine propagation finishes. Helius LaserStream ingests raw shreds and its 'preprocessed transactions' arrive ~8ms faster on average than the `processed` commitment level; published latency deltas for Helius were p50=2.92ms, p95=26.58ms, p99=45.08ms (source: shreder.xyz benchmark — note this is a competitor's benchmark of Helius, so it is adversarial; treat the absolute values as indicative not authoritative; I attempted to fetch the full benchmark page and it returned HTTP 503). Geyser gRPC vs RPC polling: ~400ms vs 2-5 seconds. blockSubscribe has documented stability problems on high-traffic programs (connection errors, skipped data) and should not be used. logsSubscribe works for pump.fun Create detection and has better cross-provider availability, but exposes less context than transactionSubscribe.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Build the detector in tiers. Baseline: Yellowstone/LaserStream gRPC transactionSubscribe with accountInclude=[pump.fun program] and failed=false, parse the Create instruction to extract mint, bondingCurve PDA, name, symbol, uri, creator. This is the best latency-per-dollar. Do NOT use blockSubscribe. Keep logsSubscribe only as a redundant failover feed on a second provider — dual-feed with dedup on signature, act on whichever arrives first. Add shreds (Jito ShredStream or Helius Raw Shreds at $1,000/mo/IP) only after you have proven profitability, since you must implement deshredding and handle the fact that shred data is pre-execution and may not land. Critically: because shreds are pre-execution, a shred-derived signal can be for a transaction that ultimately fails — always re-validate against the confirmed state before sizing up.

findings.claim: Helius Sender is the best single-integration multi-path submitter; minimum tip is documented inconsistently across Helius's own sources
findings.detail: Endpoints: https://sender.helius-rpc.com/fast (auto-routed) and /ping for connection warming. Regional HTTP for backends: slc-, ewr-, lon-, fra-, ams-, sg-, tyo-sender.helius-rpc.com/fast. Submits simultaneously across Helius, Jito, Harmonic and Rakurai pathways. Default 50 TPS, no API credits consumed, available on every plan including free. Supports sendBundle with up to 4 transactions (vs Jito's 5). Has a `?mev-protect=true` query parameter that routes around validators statistically linked to sandwich attacks. DISAGREEMENT ON MINIMUM TIP: the current Sender docs page states Sender Max minimum = 0.001 SOL (entering a priority tip buffer for top-of-block) with a cost-optimized SWQOS-only tier at 0.000005 SOL, and states tips between 0.000005 and 0.001 SOL are accepted but routed best-effort through fewer pathways. However the Helius zero-slot blog post states 0.0002 SOL, and sol-trade-sdk's constant SWQOS_MIN_TIP_HELIUS is 0.0002 with SWQOS_MIN_TIP_HELIUS_SWQOS_ONLY=0.000005. Most likely the threshold was raised from 0.0002 to 0.001; treat 0.001 SOL as current and verify at integration time.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Integrate Sender as the primary submit path — one HTTP POST gets you Jito + SWQoS + two other relays in parallel, which is far cheaper than integrating 5 relays yourself. Use the regional HTTP hostname (not the auto-routed HTTPS) from your backend, selected by the leader-region table. Run a background task hitting /ping every 2-5 seconds to keep the TCP/TLS connection warm — a cold handshake costs a full RTT. Set ?mev-protect=true on all BUY transactions. Send tip >= 1,000,000 lamports (0.001 SOL) on contested mints to enter the priority buffer; drop to the 0.000005 SOL SWQOS-only tier for non-urgent exits.

Put the tip in the SAME transaction as the buy, not a separate bundle transaction — a separate tip tx wastes a bundle slot and adds a signature. For non-bundle sends apply the documented 70/30 priority-fee/tip split.

findings.claim: Jupiter's production dynamic-slippage config gives exact bps caps per token category — pump.fun new graduates cap at 1000-2000 bps
findings.detail: From github.com/jup-ag/dynamic-slippage-config slippage_config.json, min/max basis points per category: solana 15-100, stable 10-80, lst 50-300, bluechip 50-300, default 100-1000, pump_new_graduate 500-2000, degen 500-2000, new_token 300-2000, pump_new_graduate_first_hour 1000-2000, degen_buy 1000-2500, degen_sell 1000-5000. The estimator uses real-time and historical swap data, reads token categories for both input and output mints, and applies the WORSE of the min/max heuristics between the two tokens. Jupiter's RTSE (Real-Time Slippage Estimator) is the third iteration, factoring volume, historical volatility and transaction patterns; Ultra V3 claims 34x greater sandwich protection than competitors by never selling order flow to third-party MEV searchers.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Adopt these exact bands as your slippage state machine. Buy path: new_token (age < 1 hour, still on bonding curve) = start at 300 bps, escalate to a hard ceiling of 2000 bps only after 2 consecutive slippage-exceeded failures. pump_new_graduate_first_hour = 1000 bps start, 2000 bps hard cap. Sell path gets the wider band (degen_sell up to 5000 bps) because failing to exit is strictly worse than a bad fill. CRITICAL ASYMMETRY: your slippage cap IS the sandwicher's maximum extraction. Setting 2500 bps on a buy is an open invitation to lose 25%. Prefer a computed minimum-out amount derived from the bonding curve reserves you read at detection time plus a fixed tolerance, rather than a percentage slippage — percentage slippage on an unknown post-race price is unbounded risk.

findings.claim: Sandwich attacks cost memecoin buyers $370-500M over 16 months and disproportionately target pump.fun tokens; average extraction is 0.0425 SOL per attack
findings.detail: Sandwich bots extracted between $370M and $500M from January 2024 to May 2025. The single Vpe bot generated $13.43M over 30 days (Dec 7 - Jan 5) executing 1.55 million sandwich transactions, averaging 0.0425 SOL ($8.67) profit per attack, annualizing to a projected 801,540 SOL. A January 2025 analytics review found sandwich attacks in 112 of 150 DeFi tokens traded that week; of the top 20 most-sandwiched tokens, 16 were pump.fun creations. Majority of victim transactions were Raydium swaps. Sandwich bots pay only 5-15% of extracted value out as tips and keep the rest — meaning they can outbid you on tips by a wide margin while remaining profitable. Solana has no public mempool, so sandwiching requires the attacker to see your transaction before execution: this happens via a colluding/leaking validator, a shared RPC that leaks, or shred observation. Per the Helius MEV report, the Agave 1.18 scheduler reduced reverted transactions from a peak of 75.7% of non-vote transactions in April 2024.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Layered mitigation, implement all: (1) Send buys ONLY through private paths — Jito bundles, Helius Sender with mev-protect=true, or a paid relay. Never broadcast a buy via a generic public RPC sendTransaction. (2) Use Jito bundles for the buy specifically: within a bundle your transaction cannot be sandwiched by another bundle because execution is atomic and sequential. (3) Compute minimum-out from the reserves you observed and enforce it on-chain, do not use a naive percentage. (4) Because 0.0425 SOL is the average extraction and your typical position may be 0.5-2 SOL, sandwiching is a 2-8% tax — that is larger than your tip budget, so paying 0.003 SOL for a protected path is clearly positive EV. (5) Vary your tip account and submission path so you are not fingerprintable as a predictable victim.

findings.claim: Provider pricing: Helius $49-999/mo tiers with gRPC gated at $499; Chainstack is the cheapest credible gRPC at ~$49/mo; dedicated nodes cluster at $2,200-2,900/mo
findings.detail: HELIUS: Free $0 (1M credits, 10 RPC req/sec, 1 sendTransaction/sec, LaserStream WSS only); Developer $49 (10M credits, 50/sec, 5 sendTx/sec, devnet gRPC only, staked connections + Sender available); Business $499 (100M credits, 200/sec, 50+ sendTx/sec, 5 sendBundle/sec, full mainnet LaserStream gRPC, up to 10 concurrent gRPC connections); Professional $999 (200M credits, 500/sec, up to 100 concurrent gRPC connections); Enterprise custom (1B+ credits). LaserStream Plus data add-ons (Professional): 5TB $400/mo, 10TB $750, 25TB $1,750, 50TB $3,250, 100TB $6,000; overage 2 credits per 0.1MB uncompressed; streaming credit rate reduced to 20 credits/MB (~$100/TB effective). Raw Shreds $1,000/mo per IP ($800 on Pro). Helius dedicated nodes from $2,900/mo with gRPC, bundle simulation, colocation options. LaserStream: 9 regional endpoints, auto-failover, 24-hour historical replay, 10M account-includes per stream, unlimited program filters, drop-in Yellowstone-compatible (change endpoint + token). NOTE: one source claims LaserStream is NOT Yellowstone-compatible (proprietary wire format) while Helius's own docs call it a drop-in replacement — trust Helius's docs, the contrary claim is from a competitor's marketing page. TRITON ONE: creator of Yellowstone/Dragon's Mouth, Steamboat, Old Faithful; dedicated nodes from ~$2,900/mo; pay-as-you-go from a $125 prepaid deposit usable across chains. QUICKNODE: gRPC from ~$499/mo; tier path Start -> Stream (adds Yellowstone gRPC) -> Aperture $499/mo (adds ShredStream and Aperture TxStream, which adds ~791 microseconds to median delivery). SHYFT: from $199/mo, gRPC + RabbitStream shred streaming + staked RPCs across 7 regions, multi-node failover, slot replay, unlimited streaming with no credit or bandwidth caps. CHAINSTACK: Yellowstone gRPC as an add-on from ~$49/mo for 2 concurrent streams, 7 streams on the next tier.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Recommended stack by stage. Prototype ($49-248/mo): Chainstack gRPC add-on ~$49 for detection + Helius Developer $49 for Sender submission + free Jito block engine. Production ($700-1,000/mo): Helius Business $499 (LaserStream gRPC, 10 connections, Sender at 50 TPS, sendBundle) + Shyft $199 as an independent second detection feed for redundancy. Scale ($3,000-5,000/mo): add a Triton or Helius dedicated node ~$2,900/mo colocated in Frankfurt or Amsterdam, plus Raw Shreds $800-1,000/mo/IP. Do not buy shreds before you have proven edge — the marginal 100-500ms only matters if the rest of your pipeline is already sub-50ms. Always run two providers for detection: a single-provider outage during a launch window is a total loss of the opportunity, and these providers do have incidents.

findings.claim: BlockRazor's own benchmark shows only 30-40% first-arrival rates even for the winning provider — no provider lands first consistently, which mandates fan-out
findings.detail: BlockRazor benchmark (2025-08-01, vendor-published so treat as favorable to BlockRazor): services tested were BlockRazor, bloXroute, 0Slot and Temporal. Methodology was deploying in-region and simultaneously sending DurableNonce transfer transactions to multiple providers, measuring first-arrival at the leader, filtering out Jito-route transactions to isolate the SWQoS route. Parameters: Jito tip 0.001 SOL, priority fee 0.001 SOL, sending frequency one transaction per 1.6 seconds (i.e. one per leader rotation). Results: BlockRazor Frankfurt reached the leader first in 30.12% of transactions; BlockRazor New York 39.83%. Even as the self-declared winner, that leaves 60-70% of races lost to other providers. Separately, Chorus One found 'normal' and 'slow' user categories take 10-60 seconds to inclusion without swQoS, and that swQoS materially reduces inclusion time; Helius cites Chorus One research suggesting swQoS can outperform Jito particularly when p95 latency exceeds 40 seconds.
findings.actionable_for_bot: This is the strongest single argument for parallel multi-path submission: since the best provider wins only ~40% of races in its own benchmark, submitting to N providers concurrently raises your first-arrival probability to roughly 1-(1-p)^N. Sending to 3 uncorrelated relays at ~35% each gives ~72%. Implement submission as fire-and-forget concurrent POSTs with a shared signed transaction, never sequential-with-fallback (sequential costs you a full RTT per hop, ~1 slot each). Track per-provider, per-region win rate in your own telemetry and reweight monthly — vendor benchmarks are marketing and your own numbers are the only ones that matter. Also note the 1.6s send frequency in their methodology equals exactly one leader rotation (4 slots x 400ms), confirming leader rotation is the natural unit of retry.
