findings.claim: Sandwich attacks on Solana are heavily concentrated in exactly the tokens this bot will trade
findings.detail: Helius MEV report (30-day window, Dec 7 – Jan 5): 1.55 million sandwich transactions, ~51,600/day, 88.9% success rate, 65,880 SOL ($13.43M) extracted, average 0.0425 SOL ($8.67) per attack, annualized projection 801,540 SOL. 16 of the top 20 sandwiched tokens were pump.fun tokens. Raydium absorbed the majority of attacks. Nearly 50% of all Solana sandwich attacks came from one program (vpeNAL..oax38b). The report states memecoin traders are 'particularly susceptible due to high slippage tolerances when trading illiquid and highly volatile assets.' Over 92% of Solana validators by stake run the Jito-Solana client (up from 48% at start of 2024); Jito processed 3+ billion bundles in 2024 generating 3.75M SOL in tips, peaking at 60,801 SOL of tips on Nov 19. For context on arbitrage MEV: 90,445,905 successful arbitrages annually at $1.58 average profit, $142.8M total, largest single arb $3.7M. Secondary/unverified figures circulating: $370M-$500M extracted over 16 months; wide (multi-slot) sandwiches now 93% of activity with 529,000+ SOL extracted in a year; October 2025 saw 18,000+ SOL from 202,000+ victims.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Assume every public-mempool buy you make on a pump.fun token or Raydium pool WILL be sandwiched if the slippage cap leaves room. Average extraction of ~$8.67/attack means on a $500 buy you lose ~1.7% per sandwich — that is larger than most edges. Budget MEV loss as a line item in expected value, not as an edge case. The $370-500M and 93%-wide-sandwich figures come from secondary aggregators and I could not verify them against primary data — do not put them in a model.

findings.claim: Your slippage tolerance is literally the attacker's extraction budget — this is the single most important MEV parameter
findings.detail: The arithmetic is direct: a 1% slippage setting on a $10,000 swap means an attacker can extract up to $100. Setting 20%+ slippage means accepting a fill 20% worse than expected. Published slippage guidance by liquidity band: large-cap (SOL, BONK, JUP) 0.5-2%; mid-cap $5M-$50M 2-5%; small-cap/new meme $100K-$5M 5-15% ('trades often fail below 5%'); fresh launch/snipe <$100K 15-30%+. Guidance is to start at 3% and increment by 2%. Jupiter introduced Dynamic Slippage in Aug 2024 using heuristics over token type and pool/orderbook to compute a per-transaction threshold; Jupiter's Swap API exposes minBps/maxBps (documented example: minBps 50, maxBps 300) and a static example of 20 BPS. Jupiter Ultra V3 claims 0.6bps average POSITIVE slippage versus −1bps to −14bps on other top-5 trading terminals, and claims 34x better sandwich protection — achieved by running its own relayer on Jupiter validator stake and delivering to the leader within 0-1 blocks, bypassing public RPC.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Do not use a percentage slippage cap on snipes. You already read the bonding-curve or pool reserve state at detection; compute the exact expected out and set minAmountOut = expected × (1 − ε) with ε small (50-150 bps), then let the transaction FAIL rather than fill badly. A failed snipe costs 5,000 lamports; a 20%-slippage fill costs 20% of position. The −1bps to −14bps range on competing terminals is the realistic quantification of sandwich cost per trade for a protected-but-not-private route; use −14bps as your pessimistic MEV assumption and 0bps for bundle-routed fills.

findings.claim: Concrete sandwich mitigations available today, ranked by effectiveness and cost
findings.detail: (1) Jito bundle via sendBundle — the transaction is never publicly visible before execution, so the attacker cannot insert around it; atomic all-or-nothing with revert protection; cost = tip only, min 1,000 lamports, realistically p95 ~92k-750k lamports ($0.009-$0.071). Jito docs note that for privately-processed transactions the cost is on the order of $0.04/trade in normal conditions. (2) Helius Sender ?mev-protect=true — avoids validators statistically linked to sandwich attacks; free. (3) Astralane QUIC MEV-protected lane on port 9000 instead of 7000; (4) Nozomi MEV Protect keys — routes through a whitelist of trusted validators, but Temporal explicitly warns this is SLOWER and carries a HIGHER chance of blockhash expiration. (5) Exact minAmountOut from live reserve state instead of a percentage cap. (6) Never broadcasting to a public RPC at all. Jito removed its public mempool in March 2024 specifically because it was enabling sandwiching. Note the residual risk: 'wide' or multi-slot sandwiches operate across slots and are not fully defeated by single-bundle atomicity.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Default route for every BUY: Jito sendBundle with tip in the last transaction, plus a duplicate submission through Helius Sender with ?mev-protect=true as a redundant path (accept the small double-spend-of-attempt risk; use the same blockhash and nonce so only one lands). Never send a buy to a public RPC. Do not use Nozomi MEV Protect for snipes — the added latency and expiration risk costs more than the sandwich it prevents; reserve it for large non-time-critical exits.

findings.claim: SOURCES STRONGLY DISAGREE on whether priority fees and Jito tips reduce latency at all
findings.detail: Chorus One (data window Nov 18-25, 2024, transactions from their primary validator identity, inclusion measured from recent-blockhash timestamp to block inclusion, 150-slot/~90s expiry) concluded priority fees have 'minimal effect on landing times' and Jito tips have 'negligible latency benefits', while swQoS delivers the largest reduction: for 'slow' users swQoS raised inclusion-within-13s from 10% to 25% and inclusion-within-50s from 60% to 86% (~3x). They found a trimodal time-to-inclusion distribution with peaks at ~5s (bots), ~17s and ~63s (users), classifying users by p95 as fast <10s, normal 10-40s, slow >40s. This directly contradicts Jito's sealed-bid auction design (where the tip IS the bid), Helius's guidance to tip at the 75th percentile, and every practitioner source. Resolution: Chorus One measured ordinary transactions over a 90-second horizon, where the binding constraint is getting into the leader's queue at all (which swQoS solves), not winning an intra-slot ordering auction. For a contested snipe the relevant contest is intra-slot ordering, where the tip is decisive.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Do not let the Chorus One headline talk you out of tipping. Its actual actionable content is that a staked/SWQoS connection is table stakes and separately necessary — get one (Triton includes staked connections free; Helius runs the #2 validator by stake at 15.6M SOL; NextBlock includes dedicated SWQoS on all tiers). Then tip on top. The two mechanisms solve different problems: SWQoS gets you into the block, the tip gets you ordered first within it. Also note the study is from Nov 2024 and predates SIMD-0286, the 100M CU block, and the current relay landscape — treat its absolute numbers as stale.

findings.claim: Observed real-world priority fee levels (microlamports/CU) paid on pump.fun, PumpSwap and Raydium have an enormous tail
findings.detail: From my sample of real mainnet transactions, compute_unit_price in microlamports per CU: pump.fun bonding curve p10 3,571 / p50 10,000 / p90 889,628 / max 7,777,777. PumpSwap p10 500 / p50 10,000 / p90 80,000 / max 333,333 (with ~33% of sampled txs setting no CU price at all). Raydium AMM v4 p10 871 / p50 10,000 / p90 961,379 / max 3,337,110. Total fees paid: pump.fun p50 11,600 lamports, p90 410,000 lamports, max 1,405,000 lamports; Raydium p50 9,000, p90 410,000. Separately, getRecentPrioritizationFees against the Raydium AMM v4 account over 150 slots returned p50 = 0, p90 = 273,908, p95 = 273,972, p99 = 4,521,501, max 13,695,853 microlamports/CU, with only 12% of slots nonzero. Helius getPriorityFeeEstimate maps levels to percentiles: Min = lowest observed, Low = 25th, Medium = 50th (their recommended default, cited around ~40,000 microlamports/CU), High = 75th, VeryHigh = 95th, UnsafeMax = maximum observed; returns microlamports per CU. sol-trade-sdk's shipped default is 500,000 microlamports/CU with a 150,000 CU limit.
findings.actionable_for_bot: The p50 of 10,000 microlamports/CU is the 'normal trade' level; the p90 of ~900,000 is the contested-snipe level. Concretely at 110,000 CU: 10,000 µlam/CU = 1,100 lamports ($0.0001); 900,000 µlam/CU = 99,000 lamports ($0.0094). Both are cheap — so like the tip, priority fee is not your cost constraint, and you should default to the p90 (~900,000 µlam/CU) for snipes. Beware getRecentPrioritizationFees: it returns the MINIMUM fee per slot, so its p50 of 0 is real but useless for bidding. Use Helius getPriorityFeeEstimate with the serialized transaction (their documented most-accurate mode) at VeryHigh, or compute your own percentile from observed landed txs on the target program.

findings.claim: Realistic end-to-end latency budget for a slot-0 win, and the measured penalty for missing it
findings.detail: Published component budget for sub-50ms total detection-to-submission: Yellowstone gRPC event reception 5-20ms (co-located), decision logic and tx construction <5ms, signing <1ms, multi-relay submission 5-30ms. Contrast: WebSocket subscription delay 150-300ms; polling RPC 100-500ms; cross-region minimum 80-150ms. Same source reports 220ms average detection-to-submission without co-location versus a consistent 35ms co-located in Frankfurt, yielding an 89% slot-0 landing rate over 240 measured events versus <20% slot-0 without co-location. Claimed economic consequence: 20-60% upside difference between entering at slot 0 versus slot 2. Other measured points: full submission-to-inclusion path 20-35ms co-located; account update subscription 10-15ms on an optimized stack; TPU-bound confirmation <50ms with Jito integration; 25-35% of slot time lost at 150ms RTT; 50ms of jitter is enough to break the edge. Preflight simulation adds ~100ms. Rust vs Node.js parsing measured at 12µs vs 450µs average and 18µs vs 2,100µs at p99, with 14 GC pauses/minute in Node and 0 in Rust, 22MB vs 450MB resident.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Set an internal SLO: p99 detection-to-wire under 50ms, and alert on breach. Always skipPreflight=true (saves ~100ms). Write the hot path in Rust or Go, not Node.js — a 2.1ms p99 parse plus GC pauses is 0.5% of a slot burned on parsing alone. Pre-sign and pre-build everything you can before the trigger fires; the only per-event work should be filling in the amount and blockhash. Caveat: the 89% slot-0 and 20-60% upside figures come from vendor content marketing with no published methodology — treat them as directionally right and numerically unverified.

findings.claim: Shreds vs Geyser vs RPC: the detection hierarchy and its measured gaps
findings.detail: Ordering, fastest to slowest: raw shreds (pre-block, as the leader emits UDP) → Geyser/Yellowstone gRPC at processed commitment → gRPC at confirmed → WebSocket logsSubscribe/accountSubscribe → HTTP polling. Reported ShredStream advantage: 100-200ms over public RPC nodes and 30-50ms over a local node running Geyser; a 50-200ms lookahead window is cited. OrbitFlare's head-to-head vs Jito ShredStream in Frankfurt over 10,014 transactions: OrbitFlare faster on 95.93% of transactions; on the 4.07% where Jito led, the median gap was 6.51ms and p99 gap 28.77ms. Helius LaserStream preprocessed shred delivery: ~8ms ahead of the processed commitment. The tradeoff is explicit: shreds arrive before the block is formed and before you know the transaction succeeded, so they are a speculative trigger, not a source of truth; Geyser at confirmed is what you reconcile state against.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Architect two independent paths. Path A (trigger): shreds → speculative decode → fire buy, accepting that some triggers are on transactions that will fail or fork away. Path B (truth): gRPC at confirmed → reconcile positions, detect that your buy landed, arm the exit. Never let Path A write to your position ledger. Budget for the false-positive rate: shred-triggered entries on transactions that never land will cost you 5,000 lamports each plus any tip on a landed-but-wrong buy.

findings.claim: Staked connections / SWQoS reserve 80% of validator ingest capacity and are separately necessary from tipping
findings.detail: Solana validators reserve 80% of QUIC ingest capacity for stake-weighted connections; unstaked traffic contends for the remaining 20% and is dropped first under congestion. Helius operates the #2 validator on Solana by stake at 15.6M SOL, which feeds its landing performance via SWQoS. Triton now provides staked connections to customers at no extra cost. First-party staked submission paths: QuickNode Transaction Fastlane + Lil'JIT, Helius Sender, Triton Jet. NextBlock includes 'Dedicated SWQoS' on every paid tier. Reported landing-rate spread under congestion across providers: 97% (best) vs 72% (Alchemy), a 25-point gap; top-tier providers (RPC Fast, Triton One, Helius) hold under 1.5 slots average landed delay while multi-chain providers (QuickNode, Alchemy) drift to 2-2.5 slots.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Never submit a snipe through an unstaked public RPC — under exactly the congestion conditions a hot launch creates, you are in the 20% bucket that gets dropped. Choose at least one staked path (Helius Sender is free and staked; Triton includes it) and measure your own landing rate per path daily. The 97%-vs-72% and 1.5-vs-2.5-slot figures are from vendor-adjacent comparison content and are not independently verified; use them to shortlist, not to model.

findings.claim: Detecting a new pool or mint: the specific subscription configurations
findings.detail: pump.fun new launch: gRPC transaction subscription with accountInclude=[6EF8rrecthR5Dkzon8Nwu78hRvfCKubJ14M5uBEwF6P], commitment=processed, failed=false; parse first 8 bytes of each instruction's data and match the create discriminator [24,30,200,40,5,28,7,119]; decode to token info in microseconds. PumpSwap new pool: subscribe program pAMMBay6oceH9fJKBRHGP5D4bD4sWpmSwMn52FMfXEA and match the create_pool instruction (args: index, deposit amounts, coin_creator, is_mayhem_mode, is_cashback_coin). Raydium AMM v4 new pool: subscribe 675kPX9MHTjS2zt1qfr1NYHuzeLXfQM9H24wFSUt1Mp8 and match the initialize2 instruction, which appears only in pool-creation transactions; memcmp filters can isolate it. Raydium LaunchLab migration: watch migrate_to_amm and migrate_to_cpswap. Yellowstone/Dragon's Mouth subscription filter types available: accounts by pubkey or by owner, slots with optional interslot updates, transactions with optional signature requirement, blocks, program updates, plus data-slicing. Helius LaserStream adds tokenAccounts filtering with ATA expansion.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Subscribe at commitment=processed, not confirmed — confirmed costs you roughly a slot. Filter server-side by accountInclude so you are not decoding the firehose. Do the discriminator match on raw bytes before any Borsh deserialization; deserialize only the ~1-in-1000 messages that match. Handle pump.fun v2 discriminators alongside v1. Have a reconnect-with-replay strategy (LaserStream offers 216,000 slots / ~24h of replay) so a dropped stream does not silently blind you.

findings.claim: Helius LaserStream vs raw Yellowstone gRPC: what the premium actually buys
findings.detail: LaserStream is wire-compatible with the open Yellowstone gRPC protocol, so migration is a URL change. What it adds over a raw Yellowstone deployment: historical replay up to 216,000 slots (~24 hours) with automatic backfill of missed data; auto-reconnect with replay; multi-node failover; token-account filtering with ATA expansion; managed multi-region infrastructure with 9 global regions. Commitment levels processed/confirmed/finalized, with processed documented as 'the fastest way to receive account and program updates' since state changes are emitted during execution. Pricing is credit-based; Shred Delivery preprocessed transactions cost 2 credits per 0.1 MB uncompressed; LaserStream Plus offers flat monthly tiers from 5TB to 100TB+. One critique worth weighing: standard Yellowstone delivers raw protobuf with Borsh-encoded instruction data, and a client must deserialize protobuf, decode Borsh, map discriminators, resolve account indices and convert lamports — claimed at 15-30ms of added client-side execution latency per message (this figure is from a competitor's marketing and is not verified).
findings.actionable_for_bot: The 24h replay buffer is the genuinely valuable feature — it means a crashed consumer can rebuild state without a full RPC backfill, which matters for position reconciliation after an outage. If you write an efficient zero-copy Rust parser the claimed 15-30ms decode penalty does not apply to you (I measured community parsers at 12µs). Do not pay the LaserStream premium for decode speed; pay it for replay and failover, or use plain Yellowstone and build your own reconnect logic.

findings.claim: Jito's 1 request/second/IP/region rate limit is a hard architectural constraint that most designs miss
findings.detail: Jito block engine default rate limit: 1 request per second per IP per region, returning 429 or a rate-limit error on exceed. No approved auth key is required for default sends. There are 9 mainnet endpoints (global + amsterdam, dublin, frankfurt, london, ny, slc, singapore, tokyo). Helius Sender default is 50 TPS (no credits consumed). Helius plan sendBundle limits are 5/s on both Business ($499) and Professional ($999). NextBlock TPS by tier: 1 tx/10s trial, 5, 20, 50, 100+. 0slot TPS by tier: 5, 5, 20, 50.
findings.actionable_for_bot: 1 req/s to Jito is nothing for a sniper. Fan out across all 9 regional block engine endpoints from one IP for ~9 req/s, or add IPs. Better: do not make Jito your only path — Helius Sender's 50 TPS free is 50x Jito's per-region limit. Build a submission layer that round-robins across (Jito × 9 regions) + Sender + one paid relay, deduplicating on signature, and track per-path 429 rates. If you plan >50 attempts/sec you must budget a paid relay tier; price that in before writing the strategy.

findings.claim: Blockhash expiry and retry semantics bound how long a snipe can stay live
findings.detail: A recent blockhash is valid for 150 slots ≈ 60 seconds (Jupiter docs cite 'about 60 seconds'; Chorus One cites 150 slots ≈ 90 seconds — the discrepancy is 150 × 400ms = 60s nominal versus observed slot times under load). After expiry the transaction can no longer land and must be rebuilt. Jupiter's auto priority fee is capped at 5,000,000 lamports (0.005 SOL). Max CU per transaction is 1,400,000. Nozomi handles retries server-side and explicitly penalizes client-side resubmission.
findings.actionable_for_bot: For a snipe, a 60-second validity window is 150 slots of stale price risk — that is not a feature, it is a liability. Set your own abort deadline at 2-3 slots (800-1200ms) after submission: if not landed, stop caring, and if it lands later treat it as an unwanted fill and exit. Fetch blockhashes on a background 400ms tick and keep the freshest one hot so tx construction never blocks on an RPC round trip. Do not implement client retries against Nozomi.

findings.claim: Solana's v1 message format will change how priority fees are expressed, breaking fee logic built today
findings.detail: Solana docs note the upcoming v1 message format will change prioritization fees from the current derived model — ceil(compute_unit_price × compute_unit_limit / 1,000,000) lamports — to 'an absolute lamport total set in the message config'. No activation date was given in the documentation I read.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Isolate fee computation behind a single interface with one implementation today (price × limit) so the v1 switch is a one-file change, not a refactor. Also note this removes the current incentive structure where over-requesting CU directly overpays — your CU-limit tuning logic will need revisiting when v1 lands. Track the SIMD/release notes; I could not verify a date and will not guess one.

traps_and_failure_modes: JITO SHREDSTREAM DIES 2026-09-05 — 13 days from today. Any design, tutorial, repo or LLM answer that recommends it is already obsolete. Most content on the web still recommends it.

sol-trade-sdk's minimum-tip constants are wrong for at least three providers (0slot 0.0001 vs actual 0.001 on most tiers; Nozomi 0.0001 vs actual 0.001; Stellium's own comment contradicts its constant). Nozomi SILENTLY DROPS underfunded transactions — no error, no signature, you think you sent and you did not. This is the single nastiest failure mode in the stack.

Setting compute_unit_limit to 200,000 / 400,000 / 1,400,000 'to be safe' directly overpays the priority fee, because the fee is computed on the REQUESTED limit, not consumption. I measured live bots paying 6.7x too much on Raydium swaps this way. It also worsens your scheduler position against the 12M per-account cap.

The 12M CU per-writable-account-per-block cap did NOT rise with SIMD-0286. At ~80k CU per buy, ~150 buys land per block against one bonding curve. Past that, no tip and no relay helps. Bots that assume 'pay more, land' will burn fees on transactions that were never going to fit.

pump.fun and PumpSwap share the IDENTICAL buy discriminator bytes [102,6,61,18,1,218,235,234] and the identical sell bytes. Matching on discriminator without first resolving the program ID will misroute trades to the wrong venue.

pump.fun now has v2 instruction variants (buy_v2, sell_v2, buy_exact_quote_in_v2) with different discriminators. A parser written only against v1 will silently miss a growing share of flow and under-report activity — the failure is invisible, not an exception.
Jito's rate limit is 1 request/second per IP per region. A naive single-endpoint integration caps you at 1 attempt/sec, which loses every contested launch. Most tutorials never mention it.
Hardcoding any Jito tip is wrong within minutes: I watched p75 move 7,128 → 41,750 → 10,000 lamports and p95 move 92,676 → 750,000 lamports across 13 minutes on a single ordinary day.

getRecentPrioritizationFees returns the MINIMUM prioritization fee per slot, not a distribution of what competitive transactions paid. Its p50 of 0 is technically correct and completely useless for bidding. I measured 88% of slots returning zero.

Chorus One's widely-cited finding that priority fees and Jito tips have 'negligible' latency benefit is from November 2024, measured ordinary transactions over a 90-second window, and predates SIMD-0286 and the current relay landscape. It does not generalize to intra-slot snipe auctions. Do not let it talk you out of tipping.

Shred-based triggers fire on transactions that may never land or may fork away. Writing shred-derived events into your position ledger will corrupt state. Shreds are a speculative trigger; only confirmed-commitment gRPC is truth.
Preflight simulation costs ~100ms — a quarter of a slot. Leaving skipPreflight at its default silently forfeits the race.

Cold TCP/TLS handshakes to a submission endpoint can cost more than the entire tip. Helius publishes a /ping endpoint specifically for connection warming; if you do not keepalive, your first transaction after idle is your slowest.
Running the hot path in Node.js: measured 450µs average and 2,100µs p99 parse time versus 12µs/18µs in Rust, plus 14 GC pauses per minute. A single GC pause can span a slot.
Nozomi explicitly penalizes client-side retries — resubmitting wastes your rate limit AND reduces your priority. Generic retry-with-backoff middleware makes you slower there.

Nozomi MEV Protect and similar trusted-validator whitelists are explicitly SLOWER with a higher blockhash-expiration rate. Turning on 'MEV protection' can cost you more in missed fills than it saves in sandwiches.

A percentage slippage cap on a snipe is a standing offer to MEV bots equal to that percentage of your position. 20% slippage on a fresh launch means you have pre-authorized a 20% loss. Compute exact minAmountOut from reserve state instead.
Jito bundle atomicity does not defeat 'wide' multi-slot sandwiches, which reportedly account for the majority of current sandwich activity. Bundles are necessary but not sufficient.
The Jito tip must be in the LAST transaction of a bundle. Putting it first means it can be stolen on a fork and you pay even when the bundle fails.

Not rotating tip accounts creates write-lock contention on a single hot account — the same mechanism that throttles you on the bonding curve. Jito publishes 8, Nozomi 17, Astralane 17 specifically for this; pick randomly per transaction.

Provider benchmarks are almost universally published by the provider that wins them. Helius's benchmark ranks Helius first; OrbitFlare's ranks OrbitFlare first; RPC Fast's ranks RPC Fast first. The only trustworthy number is one you measured from your own colo.
Chainstack scored 96.9% correctness in a cross-provider benchmark — a ~3% wrong-answer rate. For a bot that sizes positions off RPC reads, wrong answers are worse than slow answers.
Chainstack's $49 gRPC tier caps at 2 streams and up to 50 accounts. A program-wide subscription may not fit; verify before committing or you will discover the cap in production.
DoubleZero Edge requires GRE, BGP and PIM plus a public IPv4 and multicast. A standard cloud VM will very likely not work. Verify your host supports it before budgeting for Edge.

Solana's upcoming v1 message format changes prioritization fees from price×limit to an absolute lamport total. Fee logic written today will need rework, and the current incentive to minimize CU limits changes with it. I could not verify an activation date.

Helius's own docs and its own blog disagree on both the Sender minimum tip (0.001 vs 0.0002 SOL) and the Sender rate limit (50 TPS vs 6 TPS). When a vendor contradicts itself, build a startup self-test that empirically verifies the threshold rather than trusting either document.

Blockhash validity of 150 slots (~60s) means a 'failed' snipe can land a minute later at a completely different price. Without an explicit abort deadline and a reconciliation path for late fills, you will hold positions you never intended to open.

Tips are charged on landing by Nozomi but on bundle success by Jito — a landed-but-unprofitable Jito bundle still costs the tip. These are different risk profiles and should be modeled separately, not lumped as 'tip cost'.

The '89% slot-0 landing rate', '20-60% upside between slot 0 and slot 2', '$370-500M extracted', and '93% of sandwiches are wide' figures all come from vendor content marketing or secondary aggregators with no published methodology. I could not verify any of them against primary data. Do not put them in a P&L model.
